en: Essential Explanations of the Dhyāna Method, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva and others at the Xiāoyáo Garden in Cháng'ān during the Yáoqín dynasty.

When a practitioner first arrives wishing to receive the Dharma, the teacher, after having questioned whether the five groups of precepts are pure, should—if the practitioner has excessive lust—instruct them in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
There are two kinds of impurity:
first, that which is loathsome and repulsive; second, that which is not loathsome or repulsive.
Why is this? Sentient beings have six kinds of desire:

first, attachment to form; second, attachment to physical appearance; third, attachment to deportment; fourth, attachment to the sound of speech; fifth, attachment to smoothness and softness; and sixth, attachment to personal characteristics.

For those attached to the five kinds of sensual desire, one causes them to contemplate them with revulsion as impure; for those attached to the mark of a person, one causes them to contemplate the skeleton as the mark of a person. Furthermore, by contemplating a corpse—whether decomposed or not—one contemplates the non-decomposed state to sever two kinds of desire:
that of physical demeanor and that of speech and sound; by contemplating the decomposed state, one completely severs all six kinds of desire.
There are two kinds of practice regarding impurity:
first, contemplating the foulness and decay of a corpse, [realizing] that one's own body is as impure as a corpse and no different from it.

Having observed in this way, a sense of revulsion arises in the mind; having grasped this sign, one goes to a secluded place—whether beneath a tree or in an empty house—and contemplates impurity by means of the sign grasped. One examines everywhere throughout the body, binding the mind within so that it does not go outward; if the mind wanders and scatters, one draws it back again to the object of focus.

Second, although one does not see it with the eyes, one receives the Dharma from a teacher and, through recollection and conceptualization, observes for oneself that the body is filled with the thirty-six impure things: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, mucus, tears, saliva, spittle, sweat, filth, fat, grease, skin, membranes, flesh, muscle, tendons, veins, marrow, brain, heart, liver, spleen, kidneys, lungs, stomach, intestines, abdomen, bladder, gallbladder, phlegm, rheum, the raw digestive organs, pus, blood, feces, urine, and various worms. Such a collection of diverse impurities is conventionally designated as the "body."
Observing oneself in this manner, one should likewise observe the external body to which one is attached.

If the mind grows weary of sensual desire, then it is finished once that aversion has subsided; however, if the mind does not subside, one should apply diligent effort and reproach the mind, thinking:
"The suffering of old age, sickness, and death is extremely near at hand; life passes away as swiftly as a flash of lightning, and a human body is difficult to obtain."
A virtuous teacher is difficult to encounter; the Buddha-dharma is about to perish like a lamp at dawn. There are many afflictions that destroy fixed dharmas:
internally there are the various defilements, and externally there are the followers of Māra; the land suffers famine, and both within and without there is old age and sickness.
The power of the thief of death is exceedingly great, destroying the practice of dhyāna-concentration. My own body is fearsome; in this regard—
Among the thieves of the various afflictions (*kleśa*), not even a slight reduction has occurred; regarding the dharmas of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), nothing has been attained.
Although one wears the dharma-robes, the interior is actually empty and void, no different from a worldly person. All gates to the various evil destinies (*apāya*) stand wide open;

among all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), one has not entered right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), and regarding all unwholesome dharmas, one has not yet achieved the certainty of non-occurrence.
Having committed evil, why do I now cling to this sack of excrement and give rise to indolence, failing to apply diligent effort to subdue my mind?
This wretched body is censured by the noble ones;

it is impure and loathsome, with filth flowing from its nine orifices. To be greedily attached to such a body is no different from the beasts; to die together with them and both cast into the darkness is utterly improper.
Thus, one should whip the mind with contemplation and self-reproach, returning it to its original state.
Furthermore, at times one should also cause the mind to rejoice, thinking:

"The Buddha is the Omniscient One; he has directly taught the Way, which is easy to understand and easy to practice. He is my Great Teacher. Thus, I should not be anxious or fearful, just as there is no fear when relying upon a great king."

"The Arhats have accomplished what was to be done; they are my companions who have already been able to subdue their minds as a master subdues a slave. Their minds are fully tamed, they possess the various fruits [of the path] and mastery over the six supernormal powers. I, too, should subdue my own mind and seek to attain this state; there is only this path, and no other."
Having reflected thus, he again contemplates impurity and further rejoices, thinking to himself:

"When I first began practicing the Way, the winds of the various afflictions blew and shattered my mind. Now that I desire to attain the Way, even the most sublime five desires cannot destroy me, let alone those that are base."
For example, when the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana had attained the path of Arhatship, his former wife, accompanied by musicians and grandly adorned herself, sought to seduce him.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses:
“Your body stands with its skeletal frame, Wrapped around by skin and flesh;
Impurities fill its interior— Not a single part is a fine thing.”
A leather bag filled with excrement and urine, with nine orifices constantly discharging their contents;
like a ghost, it has no inherent value—how can you consider yourself noble?
Your body is like a moving latrine, merely covered by a thin skin.
The wise abandon you from afar, Just as a person leaves a latrine.
If people knew your body As I loathe it,
they would all avoid it, Just as one avoids a pit of excrement.
Your body is adorned with flowers, perfumes, and necklaces;
these are what the foolish crave, but the wise are not deluded by them.
You are a collection of impurities, a gathering of all manner of foul and evil things.
Just as one might decorate a latrine, the fool considers it beautiful.
Your ribs are fixed to your spine like rafters resting upon a ridgepole;
the five viscera are within your belly, as impure as a basket of excrement.
Your body is like a house of filth, cherished and loved by fools;
adorned with pearl necklaces and ornaments, it is outwardly beautiful like a painted vase.
If one wishes to defile empty space, it can never be stained from beginning to end.
You wish to come and harass me, like a moth casting itself into a flame.
All poisons of desire have now been extinguished by me;
the five sensual pleasures are already far removed, and the net of Māra is torn asunder.
"My mind is like space, entirely free from attachment;
even if celestial desires were to come, they could not defile my mind.
When a practitioner contemplates in this way with firm resolve, they abide in the fundamental object of the mind and do not fear the various desires.
If one possesses sharp faculties, by practicing with single-minded diligence, the mind may attain stable concentration after as long as seven days;
those of middling faculties may require up to three weeks;
and those of dull faculties may attain it only after a much longer period.
Just as churning curd produces butter, it is certain that one will obtain it.

If one is not fit for practice, then even if this body has long practiced various methods and analogies, one will gain nothing at all; it is like churning water, which ultimately never produces butter.
Question: In what way is it not appropriate? Answer:

If one has committed a transgression of the prohibitive precepts that cannot be expiated, or if one harbors wrong views and does not relinquish them, or if one has severed the roots of goodness, as well as the three types of concealment—namely, thick and heavy afflictions, the five crimes of immediate retribution, and the karmic retribution of the three evil realms—one should not practice such offenses.

Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties possess the causal conditions of actual wisdom and merit; their practice differs from that [of others]. If they are not yet capable of practicing the formal cultivation [of meditation], they should recite the sutras, cultivate merit by erecting stupas and making offerings, preach the Dharma to transform others, and practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
Question: How should one know the characteristics of having attained one-pointedness of mind? Answer:

Regarding the sign of the mind abiding: the body becomes supple, light, and blissful; all mental states such as anger, grief, and various afflictions have already ceased. The mind attains a happiness never before experienced, surpassing the five sensual desires. Because the mind is pure and unturbid, the body possesses radiance, like the reflection appearing on the surface of a clear mirror, or like the brilliant illumination of a bright pearl in pure water. When the practitioner perceives this sign, their mind becomes peaceful and joyful.

For example, it is like a thirsty person who digs into the earth seeking water; once they see moist mud, they know that water will not be far off. In the same way, when a practitioner first begins their practice, it is like digging through dry soil; by persevering over time, they perceive signs of moisture and know for themselves that they will soon attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

With single-minded faith and joy, he diligently restrains his mind and enters into deep meditative concentration. Having formed this thought, he reviles the five desires; seeing those who seek them as utterly loathsome—like a person who, finding no good food, eats foul excrement—he uses these various causes and conditions to condemn desire as a fault. He feels compassion for those who accept the five desires, thinking: "They have happiness within their own minds yet do not know how to seek it; instead, they seek externally the impure pleasure of sin."

The practitioner should always be diligent, gathering all wholesome dharmas day and night to assist in the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and causing the mind to remain far removed from those factors that obstruct meditation.

To gather all wholesome dharmas means to contemplate the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is like a disease, like a wound, like an abscess, and like an arrow piercing the heart. The three poisons burn fiercely, giving rise to various conflicts and the smoke-like signs of jealousy, which are exceedingly loathsome and detestable.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to be practicing the initial stage of dhyāna.

If, while practicing the Dharma, the five hindrances should at any time obscure the mind, they must be eliminated immediately, just as a black cloud obscuring the sun is dispersed by the power of the wind.
If the hindrance of sensual desire arises, and one's mind thinks of the five objects of desire, one should immediately reflect:
"I am now on the Path; having renounced the five desires myself, why do I think of them again?"

It is like a person eating back their own vomit; this is a sinful practice of the world. Now that I have studied the Way, shaving my hair and beard and donning the dharma robes, for as long as my life lasts, I have forever abandoned and forever severed the desires of the five sensual pleasures. How could I ever again give rise to attachment?
"This is most certainly inappropriate.
He immediately ordered them to be eradicated, just as one would not allow thieves or venomous snakes to enter a room, because the calamity they bring is so profound and grave.
Furthermore, the phenomena of the five desires are the dwelling place of all evils.

They lack gratitude and reciprocity; while they may be acceptable at first, after a long time they deceive others and undergo various bitter sufferings. Driven by jealousy and wrath, there is no evil they will not commit, like a bag filled with many knives that wounds and destroys both those who embrace it and those nearby when touched by hand.

Furthermore, even if one obtains the five sensual pleasures, one still does not attain satiety; if there is no satiety, there is no joy. It is like drinking thin gruel when thirsty: as long as the thirst has not been relieved, there can be no joy. It is also like scratching a scab: as long as the affliction has not been cured, it cannot be considered pleasure.

Furthermore, when the mind is stained by lust, one fails to discern the beautiful from the ugly and does not fear the retribution for sins in this life or future lives; for this reason, one must eliminate sexual desire.
Once sexual desire has been eliminated, if anger or affliction should arise, one must immediately eliminate that anger and affliction as soon as it is born in the mind.
Sentient beings are worthy of compassion:
from the moment they enter the womb until birth, there is no time when they do not suffer, being fully possessed of manifold afflictions. How could one further increase their distress?
It is like a person facing execution; what good person would inflict additional pain upon them?

Furthermore, a person practicing the Path should abandon the fetters of self-attachment, pride, and so forth; even though these do not obstruct rebirth in heaven, one practicing the Path should not give rise to such thoughts, let alone harbor anger, which uproots the very foundation of happiness.

Furthermore, just as when water is boiling and agitated, one's facial reflection cannot be seen, so too when a mind of anger arises, one fails to recognize the distinction between the noble and the humble, nor one's parents and teachers, and ultimately refuses to accept the Buddha’s teachings.
Hatred is a grave illness; its cruelty and lack of principle are like those of a rākṣasa. One should eliminate this hatred by cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Once lust and hatred have ceased, if one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), there will be joy;

but if one does not yet attain the bliss of dhyāna, the mind becomes distracted, troubled, and increasingly heavy, becoming dull and clouded. Then one realizes that sleep is a thief that harms the mind; it destroys even worldly benefits, let alone the matters of the Path.

The method of sleep is no different from death; they are distinguished only by the presence of breath. Just as when water is covered by moss one cannot see one's reflection, so too when sleep covers the mind, one does not perceive beauty or ugliness; the reality of all phenomena is likewise thus.
One should immediately remove them and reflect thus:
"All these thieves of affliction desire to cause me harm; how can I sleep peacefully?
It would be as improper to sleep while facing an enemy army amidst the clash of blades."

Not yet free from the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death, and not yet liberated from the suffering of the three evil realms, one has not attained even the stage of "warmth" within the Dharma of the Path; therefore, one should not sleep.

Having formed this thought, if sleep still does not cease, one should immediately rise and walk about, wash the face with cold water, look toward the four directions, and gaze up at the stars. One should contemplate three matters to eliminate drowsiness so that it does not overwhelm the mind:

first, fear. One should reflect for oneself that the Great King of Death possesses immense power and constantly seeks to cause harm; one should keep death in mind as being very near, like a thief approaching swiftly with nothing to rely upon, or like a drawn sword held to one's neck, which would sever one's head if one falls asleep.
Second is encouragement and consolation; one should form this thought:
"The Buddha is the Great Teacher; all his sublime Dharmas are unprecedented, and I have received and studied them."
Rejoicing in this personal good fortune, the mind of sleep immediately ceases.
Third, regarding sorrow and anxiety, one should further reflect:
"In future lives, as one transmigrates and undergoes successive births, the suffering, pain, and toxic harms will be boundless and immeasurable."
Thus, by means of various causes and conditions, one should censure the practice of sleep; when one reflects in this way, sleep will cease.
If the hindrance of restlessness and remorse arises, one should reflect thus:

"Worldly people give rise to agitation and playfulness because they wish to eliminate sorrow and seek joy. Now, I am practicing austerities, sitting in meditation, and seeking the Way; how can I indulge myself and let my mind become agitated and playful?"
This is most improper.
In the Buddha-dharma, that which is held most essential is taking the gathering of the mind as the foundation; one should not be frivolous or allow the mind to run wild and abandon itself.
Just as a face cannot be seen when water is disturbed by waves, so too, when the mind is agitated by restlessness and playfulness, its true nature—whether good or bad—is not perceived.
The explanation for regret is as described in the section on the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). Question:
Greed, ill-will, and doubt each constitute a separate hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*); why, then, are sleep and restlessness-regret combined into a single hindrance?

Answer: Although drowsiness is an affliction, its power is slight; if sleep does not assist it, it does not obscure the mind. Likewise, restlessness and remorse cannot constitute an *āvaraṇa* (hindrance) on their own. For this reason, these two are combined to form a single hindrance.
For example, when binding an object with a rope, a single strand lacks strength, but when combined, it can bind.

Furthermore, the mental factor of sleepiness arises because the sleeping mind is heavy; because the mind is heavy, the body also becomes heavy. Due to the subtle covering of sleep, the covering of torpor increases further, obstructing and destroying the factors conducive to the Path. Therefore, these two combined constitute a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Once awakened from sleep, the mind is not one-pointed; its thoughts race toward the five desires and it engages in various afflictions—this is called restlessness (*auddhatya*).
It is like a monkey that has escaped its confinement, leaping and frolicking at will among the trees and forests.

Restlessness is also like this: having already contemplated the five desires and given rise to various fetters and afflictions, one’s body, speech, and mind falter, giving birth to sorrow and regret, and one thinks to oneself:
"I have done what should not have been done, and I have failed to do what should have been done."
Therefore, restlessness and remorse, being mutually dependent, are combined to form a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*). Question:
Since one can repent for having committed evil, it should not constitute a hindrance?
Answer: If one repents for having violated the precepts and resolves from this moment forward never to do so again, it is not an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance).
However, if one commits an offense and constantly dwells upon it without ceasing, such that anxiety and distress disturb the mind, it is called a hindrance.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one should censure the hindrance of restlessness and remorse.
One should bind the mind to its object;
if doubt arises in the mind, one should immediately cause it to be extinguished.

Why is this so? Doubt as a mental state is not like craving or pride; it does not produce a joyful mind in the present life, and in future lives it causes one to fall into hell. Doubt obstructs all wholesome dharmas, just as one who hesitates at a forked road does not know which way to advance and thus simply stops.

When a practitioner is thus, if they harbor doubts regarding the dharmas they have originally practiced and no longer advance, they should immediately recognize that the affliction of doubt obscures the Right Path and must be swiftly eliminated.
They further reflect:

"The Buddha is the Omniscient One; he has distinguished all dharmas—these are worldly dharmas and these are supramundane dharmas, these are wholesome and these are unwholesome, these are beneficial and these are harmful—with perfect clarity. Now I should simply receive and practice them without giving rise to doubt; I should follow his teachings and not reject or oppose them."
Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma is sublime because its cultivation of concentration and wisdom accords with reality and the Dharma;
I lack such wisdom, so how could I use my own mind to deliberate upon all phenomena?
Just as one must wield a sharp weapon to contend with a thief, if one faces a powerful enemy without such a tool, it will instead bring harm;
likewise, how can I now wish to deliberate upon the true nature of all phenomena when I have not yet attained the wisdom of meditative concentration?
This should not be so. Furthermore, since non-Buddhists are not disciples of the Buddha, they ought to harbor doubts; how could I, being a disciple, harbor doubts regarding the Buddha?
The Buddha has always disparaged the affliction of doubt, for it is a covering and a veil, an obstruction and a hindrance—a dharma that deceives oneself.
Just as one who recognizes an assassin should immediately eliminate and avoid them, so too is doubt:
it deludes the practitioner, seeking to obstruct true wisdom with its own doubtful intellect.

For example, when one has scabies, scratching it only increases the affliction until the body is ruined; yet, if a skilled physician administers medicine, the itching ceases of its own accord. It is the same for the practitioner:

when various phenomena give rise to thoughts of doubt, the more one attempts to resolve those matters, the more the mind of doubt proliferates. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching is to directly cause one to sever doubt; as soon as doubt arises, it is immediately extinguished.
Having thus refuted various doubts in this manner, one should swiftly eliminate them.

The practitioner, contemplating in this way, abandons the five hindrances and gathers all wholesome dharmas; entering deeply into single-mindedness, they sever the afflictions of the desire realm and attain the first dhyāna concentration. As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras: "The practitioner, detached from desires and from unwholesome, evil dharmas, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna."
Question: What are the characteristics of attaining the first dhyāna? Answer:

As previously described, one first uses right mindfulness to rebuke and cease the five desires; before yet attaining the stages (*bhūmi*), the body and mind experience happiness, becoming supple, gentle, and light, and the body possesses radiance.

As the signs of the first dhyāna are attained, they become further enhanced and superior. Because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) pervade the entire body, it becomes supple, gentle, and light; because one is free from desire, evil, and unwholesome states through single-minded concentration, it brings about bliss. Since the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the form realm possesses the characteristic of radiance, the practitioner perceives a wondrous light illuminating both the interior and exterior of the body.

Thus, the practitioner’s mind undergoes a transformation: he does not feel anger toward objects that provoke anger, nor does he feel joy toward objects that provoke joy; he cannot be moved by the eight worldly dharmas. His faith, reverence, shame, and remorse increase manifold. He feels no attachment to clothing, food, drink, and the like, regarding only various wholesome merits as noble and all else as base. He does not even fixate his mind upon the five sensual desires of the heavens, let alone the impure five sensual desires of the world.
One who attains the first dhyāna possesses such signs as these.

Furthermore, at the time of attaining the first dhyāna, the mind is filled with great wonder and joy, just like a poor person who suddenly discovers a treasure trove and feels immense delight, thinking to himself:

"Through diligent and ascetic practice during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night, I have cultivated the path of the first dhyāna; now its fruit has been obtained, true and not false—such is this sublime bliss."
"Yet these sentient beings are deluded, perverse, and ignorant; they are submerged in the impurities and non-pleasures of the five desires, which is truly pitiable.

The bliss of the first dhyāna pervades both the interior and exterior of the entire body, like water soaking dry earth until it is thoroughly saturated inside and out. The physical parts of those in the desire realm cannot experience such pervasive bliss; their bodies are scorched by the fires of lust and anger. Entering the pool of the first dhyāna brings supreme coolness and joy that eliminates all burning afflictions, just as one who is suffering from extreme heat enters a refreshing, cool pond.

Having attained the first dhyāna, one recollects the gates of the path of practice previously cultivated; there may be other conditions, such as the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, or the contemplation of impurity, loving-kindness, and so forth.

Why is this so? It is because the power of this contemplative practice enables one to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and enter it ever more deeply, causing the original insight to increase manifold in its purity and clarity.

Once the practitioner has attained the first dhyāna, they proceed to seek the second dhyāna. If following the path with outflows (*sāsrava*), they come to feel weary of and distressed by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) at the threshold of the second dhyāna; just as the five desires and the five hindrances of the desire realm cause the mind to become distracted, so too do the applied and sustained thoughts of the first dhyāna disturb and agitate the concentrated mind.

If one is on the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and has abandoned the desires of the first dhyāna, one uses the untainted first dhyāna itself to censure applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Question: Since the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the first dhyāna can also disturb the mind, why is it that only applied and sustained thought are mentioned?
Answer: The fetters (saṃyojana) of the first dhyāna are called vitarka and vicāra. Why is this so?

Because attachment arises due to wholesome *vitarka* and *vicāra*, these fetters (*saṃyojana*) are also termed *vitarka* and *vicāra*. When one first attains the first dhyāna, no other attachments yet exist.

Furthermore, since one has never before experienced the great joy (*prīti*) of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, this great joy causes the concentrated mind to be ruined; because it destroys concentration, it must first be abandoned.

Furthermore, in order to enter the profound second dhyāna, one eliminates vitarka and vicāra; for the sake of a great benefit, one relinquishes a minor benefit, just as one abandons the minor pleasure of the desire realm to obtain a great pleasure.
Question: It is said only that vitarka and vicāra should be extinguished; why is it not said that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first dhyāna [should be extinguished]? Answer:
Vitarka and vicāra refer to the wholesome vitarka and vicāra of the first dhyāna.
Afflictions such as craving for the first dhyāna are also termed vitarka and vicāra; because unwholesome vitarka and vicāra obstruct the path to the second dhyāna, they should be extinguished.

Because wholesome applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) can cause the practitioner to remain and allow the mind to dwell in pleasure, they too must all be extinguished. Upon further reflection, one realizes that unwholesome applied and sustained thought are true thieves;

even wholesome applied and sustained thought, though appearing to be friends, are likewise thieves, for they rob me of my great benefit. Therefore, one should strive to seek the extinction of both types of applied and sustained thought. The disturbance caused by applied and sustained thought is like a person who, having become utterly exhausted, sleeps peacefully but is disturbed by various sounds. Thus, once the practitioner has extinguished these applied and sustained thoughts and seeks the second dhyāna, it is like wind and dust that can turbid clear water so that no reflection is seen. The five desires of the desire realm turbid the mind like dust turbid water, and the distraction of applied and sustained thought disturbs the mind like wind agitating water. Because applied and sustained thought are extinguished, one attains internal purity; free from applied and sustained thought, one enters the second dhyāna born of concentration, characterized by joy and bliss.
Question: What are the characteristics of the second dhyāna? Answer:

The Sūtra states: "Having extinguished all discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and investigations (*vicāra*), whether wholesome or neutral, because the mind is unmoved by such discursiveness, the inner mind becomes pure. It is like water that is clear and still, free from wind and waves, wherein the stars, the moon, and the mountains are all clearly visible. Because the inner mind is thus purified, it is called the 'sage’s silence' (*ārya-tūṣṇīmbhāva*)."

Although the third and fourth dhyānas are both silent, because the second dhyāna is first attained, it is designated as having vitarka and vicāra—the causes and conditions for speech; since these causes and conditions have just ceased, it is named "silence."

The sublime and excellent first dhyāna is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss; the joy and bliss of the first dhyāna arise from the abandonment of desire, and herein the joy and bliss arise from the meditative concentration of the first dhyāna.
Question: The second dhyāna also abandons the fetters and latent tendencies of the first dhyāna; why, then, is it not said that [its bliss] arises from abandonment?
Answer: Although one is indeed free from the fetters (*saṃyojana*), because the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is predominant, it is designated by the name of that concentration.

Furthermore, to say "free from desire" means being free from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); to say "free from the first dhyāna" does not mean being free from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Therefore, it is not called "freedom from birth. Such characteristics as these belong to the second dhyāna.

Once the practitioner has attained the second dhyāna, they further seek a deeper concentration. However, the second dhyāna concentration is obscured by afflictions—namely craving, pride, false views, and doubt—which destroy the concentrated mind. These are the "thieves" of the second dhyāna that block the gateway to the third dhyāna; therefore, one should seek to eradicate these defects in order to attain the third dhyāna.
Question: If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha say that one enters the third dhyāna by being detached from joy and dwelling in equanimity? Answer:

Upon attaining the second dhyāna, there is great joy (*prīti*). When the mind of joy becomes excessive, it undergoes transformation and becomes attached to joy, thereby giving rise to various fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). For this reason, joy is the root of affliction.

Furthermore, since the various fetters and latent tendencies offer no benefit, one should not give rise to attachment toward them; yet joy is a source of delight that is highly beneficial, and because it is so deeply clung to and difficult to relinquish, the Buddha taught that by abandoning joy, one enters the third dhyāna.

Question: Since the five desires are impure and sinful, one should abandon delight in them; yet this delight is pure, subtle, and what sentient beings enjoy—why, then, do you say it should be abandoned? Answer:
I have already answered that the causes and conditions for the arising of attachment are themselves the gateways to transgression.
Furthermore, if one does not relinquish joy, one cannot attain supreme and wondrous merit; for this reason, what fault could there be in relinquishing the small to obtain the great?

The practitioner advances to seek the third dhyāna. Observing joy (*prīti*), he recognizes its peril: that which is delightful through the conditions of mental affliction and suffering is subject to impermanence and change, thereby giving rise to sorrow and pain.

Furthermore, joy is a coarse pleasure; now, wishing to abandon the coarse in order to seek subtle pleasure, he is said to "leave joy behind" and enter a deeper concentration to seek the bliss of a distinct meditative state.
What is the cessation of joy through the characteristics of the third dhyāna?

One abandons this sublime joy so that the mind feels no regret or longing; one recognizes joy as a source of harm. It is like a person who, knowing his wife to be a rākṣasī, is able to abandon her without regret or longing. Joy is a coarse phenomenon of madness and delusion, not something sublime. In the third dhyāna, the body experiences bliss—the most supreme bliss in the world, beyond which there is none—and it is that which the noble ones traverse. Being able both to experience and to relinquish the bliss free from joy, one thoroughly enters the third dhyāna with a body characterized by mindfulness and skillful wisdom.
Question: This teaching speaks of the wisdom of one-pointed mindfulness; why are the first and second dhyānas not mentioned? Answer:

Regarding the third dhyāna: the body experiences pervasive bliss while the mind practices the dharma of equanimity (*upekṣā*), ensuring that the mind does not become attached to or differentiate between the pleasant and the unpleasant; therefore, it is said that "the mind is one-pointed with mindfulness and wisdom."
Furthermore, within the third dhyāna there are three faults:
first, the mind becomes excessively subtle and sinks; second, the mind becomes greatly agitated; and third, the mind becomes confused and faints.

The practitioner should always single-mindedly contemplate these three faults. When the mind sinks, one should use the power of diligence and wisdom to cause it to rise again; when it is excessively agitated, one should restrain and calm it; when the mind is confused or distressed, one should recollect the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma to restore joy to the mind. One should constantly guard and treat these three states of mind; this is called the practitioner who delights in single-minded practice entering the third dhyāna.
Question: According to the Sūtra, two types of bliss are spoken of within the third dhyāna; what are these two kinds of bliss? Answer:
Previously, "feeling pleasure" was mentioned; subsequently, "blissful happiness" was mentioned. Question:
There are three kinds of pleasure:
There is the pleasure of sensation, the pleasure of joy, and the pleasure of being free from affliction.
For what reason is the third dhyāna called the foremost pleasure?
The answer is:

The three types of bliss are all superior and sublime compared to the lower stages; however, because the first type—experiential bliss—is preeminent and reaches ultimate perfection therein, it alone is designated as the "Stage of Bliss.
As for the other two types of bliss, they still exist in the higher stages, but they are not used as the name for this stage.
Question: What is the difference between joy (prīti), pleasure (sukha), and the absence of joy and pleasure? Answer:
There are two kinds of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*):
first, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and second, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
The faculty of joy is associated with the bliss of joy and is subsumed under the first and second dhyānas.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is devoid of joy (*prīti*) and is subsumed under the third dhyāna.

Furthermore, within the desire realm and the first dhyāna, coarse pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is termed the faculty of pleasure, while subtle pleasant feeling is termed the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*);
in the second and third dhyānas, coarse pleasant feeling is the faculty of joy, while subtle pleasant feeling is the faculty of pleasure.
For example, when one is extremely hot, obtaining clear, cool water to wash one's hands and face is called joy;
entering a great cool pond to bathe the entire body is called experiencing pleasure.

The practitioner is thus: because of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) in the first dhyāna, bliss does not pervade the body; because of the agitation of great joy (*prīti*) in the second dhyāna, it cannot pervade the body; in the third dhyāna, because there are no such obstacles, bliss pervades the entire body—this is called the distinction.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*):
the pleasure associated with the six consciousnesses of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and is also called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*);
the pleasure associated with the four consciousnesses of the first dhyāna is called the faculty of pleasure and is also called the faculty of joy.
The pleasant sensation associated with the mental consciousness in the second dhyāna is termed the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*);
because of the departure from joy in the third dhyāna, the pleasant sensation associated with the mental consciousness is termed the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Once the practitioner has attained the third dhyāna and perceives the three superior joys, he guards them with single-mindedness, constantly fearing their loss; this constitutes an affliction.
Therefore, even joy becomes a source of suffering, and one should seek liberation from it.

For example, when a person seeks the pleasure of wealth and status, the seeking itself is suffering; once obtained, the lack of satiety is suffering; and having obtained it, the guarding and protecting of it is likewise suffering.

Some abandon pleasure because they perceive the pursuit of it as suffering; some abandon it because, despite having attained pleasure, they feel no satiety and perceive it as suffering; and some abandon it because, once it has been attained, they perceive its preservation as suffering.

The practitioner’s aversion to pleasure is likewise: they abandon the pleasure of the first dhyāna because it is disturbed by vitarka and vicāra; they abandon the second dhyāna because of the agitation caused by great joy (prīti); and they abandon the third dhyāna because they know its pleasure is impermanent and difficult to maintain. For this reason, one should abandon these pleasures and seek the secure ground of the fourth dhyāna.
Question: A practitioner relies on the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to abandon sensual pleasure; now, by relying on what do they abandon the bliss of meditation?
If they abandon the bliss of meditation, what benefit is obtained?
The answer is:

The practitioner, relying on the bliss of nirvana, is able to relinquish the bliss of dhyāna because they attain three benefits—namely, the paths of the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha. Therefore, they relinquish the bliss of meditative concentration and practice the peaceful and joyful states of the four dhyānas, entering nirvana at will by means of the three vehicles.
Question: How is one to know the characteristics of this fourth dhyāna? Answer:

As the Buddha has taught the characteristics of the four dhyānas: if a bhikṣu abandons pleasure and abandons pain, and first extinguishes sorrow and joy, he enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity through mindfulness and equanimity.

Question: It is appropriate that the bliss of the third dhyāna is abandoned; since suffering has already been abandoned at the time of detachment from desire, why is it stated again here that suffering is abandoned? Answer:
Some say that there are two kinds of abandonment:

first, abandonment by specific characteristics; second, abandonment by general characteristics. For example, the *srotāpanna* abandons all fetters and afflictions pertaining to the vision of the truths through the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) in its general aspect.
This is not the case. Why?

Because the Buddha taught that suffering and pleasure are abandoned first, followed by the cessation of grief and joy. If it were the suffering of the desire realm, he should have said that suffering, grief, and joy are abandoned first; since he did not say so, we know it is not the suffering of the desire realm.
Because the mark of impermanence in the bliss of the third dhyāna gives rise to suffering, it is said that one must abandon suffering.

Furthermore, as the Buddha taught, when experiencing pleasant feeling, one should contemplate it as suffering; for the arising and abiding of the bliss in the third dhyāna constitute pleasure, while its cessation constitutes suffering. For this reason, it is said that one must abandon both pleasure and suffering.
Regarding the phrase "first extinguishing sorrow and joy": this refers to sorrow within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and joy in the first two dhyānas.

Question: Within the desire realm there is both suffering (*duḥkha*) and sorrow; these are extinguished at the time of detachment from desire. Why, then, is it said only that sorrow is severed, and not that suffering is severed?

Answer: Although both [faculties] are severed at the time of detachment from desire, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is no longer actualized, whereas the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) remains actualized; because it is still actualized, one cannot say that it has been extinguished.

Question: If the pleasure within the third dhyāna is pleasant when arising and abiding, but becomes suffering at the time of its cessation, why is it that the joy within the first and second dhyānas is not likewise described?

Answer: As stated in the Buddhist sūtras, it is at the time of departing from the third dhyāna that one abandons pleasure and abandons pain, and brings about the cessation of sorrow and joy; this is not said regarding the first and second dhyānas.
Question: For what reason did the Buddha not make such a statement? Answer:

The bliss within the third dhyāna is the most exquisite among all experiences of pleasure within the three realms. Because the mind is attached to it, that attachment causes suffering through impermanence. Furthermore, because joy (*prīti*) is coarse, it cannot permeate the entire body; thus, even when it is lost, it does not give rise to great distress. For this reason, the Buddha’s sūtras do not mention it.

Regarding "neither-painful-nor-pleasant": although there is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling within the fourth dhyāna, "equanimity" (upekṣā) refers to the relinquishing of the bliss of the third dhyāna; one practices the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling without recollection or regret.
Regarding "purity of mindfulness" (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*): mindfulness is pure because the four matters of sorrow, joy, suffering, and pleasure have been extinguished. Question:
Why is purity not mentioned in the [descriptions of] the three higher dhyānas, yet mentioned here alone?
The answer is:

In the first dhyāna, because it is disturbed by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), mindfulness is not pure. It is like lighting a lamp in the open air; although there is oil and a wick, the light cannot illuminate because it is blown by the wind.

In the second dhyāna, although it is unified by a single consciousness, the mind of concentration is distracted because joy (*prīti*) arises intensely; therefore, it is not called "purity of mindfulness."
In the third dhyāna, the mind is largely attached to pleasure, which disturbs this meditative concentration; therefore, "purity of mindfulness" is not mentioned.
In the fourth dhyāna, however, none of these things exist; hence it is said that mindfulness is pure.

Furthermore, although the lower stages possess a concentrated mind, because of the presence of inhalation and exhalation, the mind is difficult to collect; since these breaths are absent therein, the mind is easily collected, and because it is easily collected, mindfulness becomes pure.

Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna is called the "true dhyāna," while the other three dhyānas are merely preparatory stages. This fourth dhyāna is like a mountain peak, whereas the concentrations of the other three dhyānas are like the paths leading up the mountain. For this reason, the Buddha has described the fourth dhyāna as the "unshakable state" (*āneñjya-sthāna*), because there is no concentration therein that can cause it to be moved; it is characterized by being a state of peace, security, and perfect composure. These are the characteristics of the fourth dhyāna.

For example, just as a skilled charioteer can bring a well-trained horse wherever he wishes, so too when a practitioner attains this fourth dhyāna, if he wishes to practice the four immeasurables, they are easily attained at will; if he wishes to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, they are easy to cultivate; if he wishes to realize the four noble truths, they are not difficult to attain quickly; if he wishes to enter the four formless absorptions, he can easily enter them; and if he wishes to attain the six supernormal powers, seeking them is likewise easy.

Why is this? In the fourth dhyāna, there is neither suffering nor pleasure; equanimity and mindfulness are pure, supple, and compliant with one's will. As the Buddha said in a parable: when a goldsmith refines gold by smelting and tempering it according to the proper method, he can fashion any vessel he desires and it will be successfully accomplished.
Question: How does a practitioner attain immeasurable loving-kindness? Answer:

Having relied upon the four dhyānas, the practitioner contemplates the sentient beings of a single city, wishing for them to attain happiness. In this same manner, he extends his thoughts to a single kingdom, the four continents of Jambudvīpa, a small thousandfold world system, a medium two-thousandfold world system, a great trichiliocosm, and even to the infinite and boundless sentient beings throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, covering them all with a heart of loving-kindness and wishing that they all attain happiness.

For example, when the kalpa of water is exhausted and the fire- and water-extinguishing jewels have vanished so that they no longer appear, the Great Ocean Dragon King’s mind is greatly stirred; from his thought, water arises and flows forth until the ocean overflows, and as the heavens pour down rain, it fills the entire world, at which time heaven and earth are so drenched that there is nowhere it does not overflow.

The practitioner is likewise: with the water of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), they extinguish hatred; the fire-gem of aversion is dissolved, and the water of compassion overflows, gradually expanding until it reaches immeasurable and boundless sentient beings. All receive its moistening benefit, which flows forth constantly and without interruption. Whether by listening to the preaching of the Dharma to further increase their compassionate mind, or like a great rain that leaves no place untouched, the practitioner’s compassionate mindfulness causes sentient beings to attain the pure happiness of the world. Furthermore, they take the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) they have attained and bestow it upon sentient beings; they also vow to grant them the bliss of the exhaustion of suffering in *nirvāṇa*, up to the supreme, ultimate bliss of all Buddhas. By the power of this compassion, all sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence in the ten directions are seen to receive this happiness.
Question: As stated in the Abhidharma, what is the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) that contemplates all sentient beings and perceives them all as experiencing happiness?

Furthermore, the sūtras speak of the samādhi of a compassionate mind that pervades the ten directions and perceives all beings as experiencing happiness; why then do you say only, "May sentient beings obtain happiness"?
The answer is:

When first practicing the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one vows that all beings may obtain happiness. Once one has deeply entered the samādhi of loving-kindness, one sees that there are no sentient beings who do not receive happiness.
It is like drilling wood to produce fire: at first it ignites fine, soft, dry grass; as the power of the fire increases, the damp wood, the forests, and the mountains are all ignited at once.

Compassion (*maitrī*) is also like this. When first entering the contemplation, one sees beings experiencing happiness and wishes that those who suffer might obtain it; through the power of compassion, this is transformed so that one sees them all actually obtaining happiness.
Question: Sentient beings do not truly have anyone who obtains [happiness]; how is it that one sees them all obtaining happiness without falling into error?
Answer: There are two kinds of concentration:
first, contemplating the true reality of all phenomena; second, contemplating the functional utility of phenomena.
For example, there are pearl merchants: first, those who are skilled in discerning the characteristics of pearls—whether they are noble or base, beautiful or ugly;

second, those who are skilled in treating and utilizing them. Some may know their characteristics but cannot utilize them; some may be able to treat and utilize them but do not know their characteristics; and some may both know their characteristics and be able to treat and utilize them.

It is the same for the practitioner: although noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire are able to contemplate the characteristics of phenomena such as the Four Noble Truths, they cannot yet apply them because they do not practice the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). This is like an ordinary person who, having abandoned desire and practicing various merits, is able to produce the four immeasurable minds through their utility, yet cannot contemplate the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Conversely, it is like Arhats liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), who are able to contemplate the true nature and, being endowed with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), give rise to the four immeasurables.
The four immeasurables are dharmas for attaining liberation; because they are beneficial, they are not inverted.

Furthermore, in the reality of the Buddha-dharma, there are no sentient beings; how then could one who contemplates suffering be considered real, while one who contemplates pleasure be considered inverted?

What is called "inversion" refers to clinging to the mark of a self amidst that which is devoid of sentient beings—whether regarding it as permanent or impermanent, finite or infinite, and so forth; this constitutes inversion.

One who practices loving-kindness knows that sentient beings are merely provisional designations; just as the combination of wheels and other parts is designated as a "chariot," so too is it with sentient beings. Therefore, when the practitioner’s mind of loving-kindness is pure, it is not inverted.

Furthermore, if sentient beings did not exist as a reality, then the experience of pleasure by sentient beings would be a perversion; yet both "there are sentient beings" and "there are no sentient beings" are extremes, and it should not be the case that only "there are sentient beings" constitutes a perversion.

Furthermore, by the power of the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the practitioner perceives all sentient beings as obtaining happiness, just as in the meditative observation of the "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*); and by the power of dhyāna-concentration, one can transform a perceived object from blue to red—how much more so that one would not see the mark of happiness inherent in all sentient beings?

Just as among those of high or low station, the poor or the wealthy, and even among the species of birds and beasts, each has its own pleasures and feels mutual compassion; the afflictions of the noble are not shared by the poor, and the afflictions of the poor are not shared by the noble.
Question: This may be so for other realms, but how is it regarding hell? Answer:

Sentient beings in the hells also possess a portion of pleasure. When they see from afar mountains of knives or rivers of ash, they all perceive them as forests or water and give rise to thoughts of pleasure; seeing women upon the trees, they likewise give rise to thoughts of pleasure. Furthermore, because their minds are inverted, they feel attachment and delight toward their own bodies. Yet when they wish to kill [the guards], they flee, wailing and begging the hell-wardens to release them; if one were to say to them, "I pardon you," and they were thus freed from this suffering of mind, that too would be pleasure. Such instances as these all constitute a portion of pleasure.

Furthermore, by means of the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), they practice a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to teach and transform sentient beings in various ways so that they may attain happiness; or they provide them with whatever they possess, as well as assisting in their benefit through the actions of body and speech. Just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of their profound heart of affection, destroy all evil realms and truly cause sentient beings to obtain various forms of happiness, for this reason, they do not merely wish for others to have it, but actually cause them to obtain happiness.
Question: What merit does one who practices loving-kindness obtain? Answer:

One who practices loving-kindness cannot be harmed by any evil, just as external thieves cannot harm one who maintains good defenses; if they wish to cause distress or injury, they instead incur calamity themselves.
It is like a person striking a spear with their palm: the palm is wounded and destroyed, while the spear remains unharmed.
Five kinds of wrong speech cannot corrupt the mind; these five are: first, speaking falsehoods;
second, speaking with harsh words; third, speaking at an improper time; fourth, speaking with an evil mind; and fifth, speaking what is not beneficial.
For example, just as the great earth cannot be destroyed, it cannot be ruined by various forms of anger, affliction, slander, and the like.
Just as empty space cannot be harmed, his mental faculty is supple and gentle, like a celestial garment.

Furthermore, when the practitioner enters into loving-kindness (*maitrī*), tigers, wolves, venomous beasts, snakes, vipers, and their like are all unable to cause harm; it is as if they have entered a fortified city where no one can inflict injury. They attain such immeasurable merits as these.
Question: Such are the virtues of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); what is called the "dharma of loving-kindness"? Answer:

The mental state that regards all sentient beings with affection and perceives them as receiving happiness—this factor associated with the mind, subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), is called the dharma of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It is either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*);

it is a mental derivative (*caitasika-dharma*), co-arising with the mind, following the mind, non-material (*arūpa*), not itself karma, yet associated with karma, co-arising with karma, and following karma.
Karmic formations are not born of retribution; they are to be cultivated, attained through cultivation, and practiced through cultivation;
they are to be realized, realized bodily, and realized through wisdom; they are either to be abandoned by reflection or not abandoned;
they are either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra; or they are with joy or without joy.
Whether there is inhalation and exhalation or no inhalation and exhalation; whether one is a noble or an ordinary person;
whether it is associated with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it does not first take the signs as its object and subsequently take phenomena as its object;
and whether it exists in the fourth dhyāna or other stages—it is called "immeasurable" because it takes immeasurable sentient beings as its object.

Because it is pure, because it is characterized by loving-kindness, and because it seeks to bring compassion and benefit, it is called the Brahma-conduct and the Brahma-vehicle; because it can reach the Brahma-world, it is called the Brahma-path, which has been the path constantly traversed by all Buddhas of the past.
Question: How does one cultivate a mind of loving-kindness? Answer:
If a practitioner thinks:
"I have shaved off my hair and beard, not for the sake of ornamentation, but to manifest the sign of having destroyed pride; since I am thus designated, I ought to practice loving-kindness.
Now that I wear dyed robes, I should practice loving-kindness so as to keep the mind unstained, and when eating the food of others, I must not receive such alms in vain."

As it is said in the Sūtra: "If there is a bhikṣu who gradually cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he follows the Buddha’s teaching; thus, he does not consume the faithful offerings of others in vain.
Furthermore, whether one is a renunciant or a lay practitioner, if they form this thought:

"By the power of the mind of loving-kindness, I shall dwell in peace and freedom from affliction amidst this degenerate age; alone among those who have broken the Dharma, I shall follow the practice of the Dharma; and I shall cause my mind to become cool and clear amidst the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*), like a refreshing pool near a village."

Furthermore, by the power of practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), enemies and those who would inflict poison or harm can no longer cause injury; it is like wearing leather sandals, where thorns cannot wound. Although a practitioner dwells within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), which abounds in anger, malice, strife, resentment, and various forms of harm, they cannot be wounded or damaged by them due to the power of the mind of loving-kindness. This is like a strong man wearing a diamond armor and wielding sharp weapons; even when entering a great battle, he cannot be harmed or destroyed.

Furthermore, this loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is capable of benefiting three kinds of people: when ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) practice loving-kindness, they eliminate all hatred and anger, thereby attaining immeasurable merit and giving rise to pure fruits; among worldly merits and virtues, none surpasses this.

For those seeking the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can destroy the abundant anger of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); other afflictions (*kleśa*) likewise perish accordingly, and one attains freedom from desire in the desire realm while gradually emerging from the three realms. As the Buddha has taught, one should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) in close proximity with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
The Mahāyāna resolve to bring sentient beings across is rooted in loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Such a mind of loving-kindness brings immeasurable benefit to three kinds of persons.
Furthermore, one practices the initial gateway of loving-kindness, employs the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) to swiftly attain it, makes it firm, and constantly cultivates it:

First, purity of ethical discipline; second, absence of remorse in the mind; third, the arising of joy within wholesome dharmas; fourth, happiness; fifth, the restraint and protection of the five sensory faculties; sixth, mindfulness of skillful wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*); seventh, detachment of body and detachment of mind; eighth, dwelling together with those of like practice; ninth, whether listening or speaking, acting in accordance with the Dharma of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); tenth, not disturbing or vexing others; eleventh, moderation in eating; twelfth, little sleep; thirteenth, sparing of speech; fourteenth, the four bodily postures being peaceful, stable, and agreeable; fifteenth, having no lack of necessary requisites according to one's needs; sixteenth, refraining from frivolous discourse regarding all phenomena.
These sixteen dharmas assist the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).

One who possesses compassion observes the suffering of sentient beings—such as the sufferings of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and worldly criminals, including hunger, cold, and illness—and because they grasp these characteristics of suffering, their compassionate heart increases further until they perceive suffering even in those who appear happy.
Question: How is it that pleasure is considered suffering? Answer:
Pleasure is impermanent; pleasure is never satiated and arises from causes and conditions. It arises and perishes moment by moment, having no time of abiding; for this reason, it is suffering.
Furthermore, as when the gods of the desire realm experience pleasure, they are like the insane or the intoxicated, lacking any discernment, and only realize [the truth] at the time of death.

As for sentient beings in the realms of form and formlessness, they become attached to the savoring of deep meditative concentrations; when their lives end, they again undergo retribution according to the causes and conditions of their karma. For such sentient beings, what pleasure could there possibly be?

The hells and the three evil realms are one's original dwelling places; existence among devas and humans is like a temporary sojourn as a guest, providing only a brief respite. For this reason, the Buddha has taught only the Truth of Suffering and not a Truth of Pleasure; therefore, there is no sentient being who does not experience suffering.

Sentient beings are pitiable; unaware of true suffering, they conceive the notion of pleasure amidst perversion. In both this life and future lives, they undergo various forms of grief and affliction without ever feeling weary of it. Although they briefly escape suffering, they return again to seek pleasure by performing all manner of painful deeds. Reflecting thus, one sees that all sentient beings are entirely subject to suffering; this is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).
The meaning of the remaining [immeasurable] compassion is as explained in the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* among the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).

As for sympathetic joy (*muditā*): the practitioner knows the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; they contemplate suffering sentient beings as having the aspect of happiness, and contemplate happy sentient beings as having the aspect of suffering. Thus, all phenomena have no fixed characteristic and revolve according to the power of the mind. If all phenomena lack any fixed characteristic, then even attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* would not be difficult, let alone other paths.
Because they can be attained at will, the mind gives rise to joy.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects:

"By means of maintaining even a small amount of precepts, diligence, and so forth, I have been able to leave desire behind and attain the immeasurable merit of the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*)."

Because he recollects all his virtuous merits, his heart gives rise to joy, just as a merchant who has carried a small amount of goods and gained a hundred-thousandfold profit feels great joy in his heart.
Again, he thought:

"Such benefits from the Dharma all arise from the grace of the Buddha. The Buddha spontaneously attained the Way and expounded it for others; by practicing according to his teachings, one obtains such benefits."

At that time, he brings to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions, whose bodies are adorned with the golden hue and the marks and signs of excellence, as well as the Dharma-body endowed with immeasurable meritorious qualities such as the ten powers; through this mindfulness of the Buddha, his heart gives rise to joy.
Furthermore, among the ninety-six types of paths, the Buddha-dharma is the most supreme; it can extinguish all suffering and lead to eternal bliss, causing the heart to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, one further distinguishes three kinds of Buddha-dharma:
first, the immeasurable and eternal aspect of nirvāṇa, which is the ultimate and indestructible dharma;
second, the eightfold noble path as the skillful means to nirvāṇa; [and third, the dharma-body of the Tathāgata].
Third, the twelve divisions of the scriptures proclaim the Eightfold Path.
Thus, by recollecting the Dharma, joy arises in the mind.

Furthermore, being able to know such true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one practices the right path and leaves behind all deviant ways; this is what constitutes a "righteous person," namely, the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, who are the foremost among all assemblies.
He reflects to himself:
"I am now among this assembly; they are my true companions and can benefit me.
For these reasons, joy arises in his heart, and he makes the aspiration that all sentient beings may likewise be filled with joy.
Because it is transformed through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one perceives that all sentient beings have attained this joy.

As for equanimity (*upekṣā*), when the practitioner is slightly weary and the mind momentarily comes to rest, they contemplate only the single characteristic of sentient beings without observing their suffering or pleasure. The characteristic of joy is like that of a small child: if one constantly dotes on them, they become spoiled and ruined; if one constantly oppresses them with hardship, they become fearful and emaciated. Therefore, at times one must practice relinquishment, neither loving nor hating.

For the practitioner who acts in this way, if they constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), they will become negligent because of the abundance of joy; if they constantly practice a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), they will give rise to sorrow and affliction because of the abundance of thoughts regarding suffering. Therefore, one should practice equanimity (*upekṣā*) so that neither suffering nor joy exceeds their proper measure.

Furthermore, when a practitioner enters the Path and attains the flavor of dhyāna-concentration, they distinguish between the beauty and ugliness of sentient beings, as well as what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. They feel respect and affection for those who are wholesome, yet give rise to contempt and disdain for those who are unwholesome—just as a person who has obtained great treasures might look upon the poor with disdain while feeling respect and affection for those who possess wealth. To destroy these two dualistic marks, one practices the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

As it is said in the sūtras: by practicing the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one eliminates and destroys hatred; by practicing the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one eliminates the affliction of sentient beings; by practicing the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one eliminates and destroys sorrow and anxiety; and by practicing the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one eliminates and destroys both aversion and attachment.
However, because one observes sentient beings attaining liberation, one acts according to the mind; this is like a person observing a forest rather than individual trees.
Furthermore, when worldly people obtain warmth in the cold or coolness in the heat, such that their livelihood accords with their wishes, this is called "pleasure" (sukha);
if they attain official rank, treasures, singing, dancing, and merriment, this is called "joy" (prīti).
If one loses these various matters, it is called sorrow and suffering;
if these three matters are absent, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The practitioner is likewise endowed with these four mental states: they experience happiness themselves and wish for sentient beings to do so as well. Once the mind has become supple, they see all sentient beings fully attaining this happiness.

Furthermore, seeing the various noble and wealthy beings in the heavens and the world, one takes up their marks of happiness and vows for sentient beings; with a mind already softened, one sees all sentient beings fully attaining such happiness. When practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great joy arises in the mind, and by means of this great joy, one vows to give it to sentient beings.

Whether arising from meditative concentration to pay homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, praising and making offerings, one likewise attains mental joy and vows to give it to sentient beings, or takes external joy and vows to give it to them. At times, one personally perceives one's own suffering—old age, illness, grief, affliction, hunger, cold, and hardship—and desires to cause sentient beings to be free from such distress. I am able to discern and deliberate upon this, yet my own mind finds even this [contemplation] painful; how much more so for sentient beings who lack wisdom and must endure manifold sufferings—how could they not be distressed?
Then, one gives rise to a mind of compassion.

Furthermore, seeing outsiders being executed, flogged, or whipped, and hearing the sutras describe the agonies of the evil realms, one grasps these characteristics of suffering and contemplates that all things are suffering, thereby giving rise to a mind of compassion.

As for equanimity (*upekṣā*), one personally abandons both aversion and affection, and likewise observes that sentient beings possess neither aversion nor affection. Furthermore, regarding external sentient beings who experience neither suffering nor pleasure—from the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as during times of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure in the desire realm—one grasps this mark and observes all sentient beings, seeing that they likewise universally experience neither suffering nor pleasure.

Furthermore, it is like a nobleman who has but one son; his love and affection for him are profound, and he is constantly compassionate toward him. He desires that the nobleman obtain every worldly pleasure, and whatever he can obtain for himself, he also bestows upon him.

If that son should at times encounter various afflictions and sufferings, the father feels profound compassion for him; yet if the son is able to escape them through his own causes and conditions, the father is greatly rejoiced. Having given rise to this joy, he immediately lets him go, allowing the son to grow on his own, so that the father may find rest.

The practitioner likewise, within the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), regards all sentient beings as if they were their own children; according to whatever joys they themselves possess and by taking up the various pleasures of the world, they vow that all beings may obtain them. By the power of the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), they perceive all of them as being joyful.

The practitioner arises from the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). If they see sentient beings undergoing various sufferings, having grasped this sign, they give rise to the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).

By the power of the mind of compassion, they see that all sentient beings are suffering; having seen them suffering, they vow to cause all sentient beings to be free from this suffering. Arising from the samādhi of compassion, if they see sentient beings receiving happiness, attaining the Way, and entering nirvāṇa, having grasped this sign, they give rise to the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Desiring that others obtain what they seek and that they obtain it themselves, their mental consciousness becomes supple, and they see all sentient beings attain joy.

Arising from this meditative concentration, they see those sentient beings who are neither in pain nor pleasure, neither sorrowful nor joyful; having grasped these signs, they give rise to an equanimous mind, vowing that sentient beings may be neither in pain nor pleasure, neither sorrowful nor joyful. Because they have skillfully cultivated the power of the concentration of equanimity, they see all sentient beings as neither in pain nor pleasure, neither sorrowful nor joyful, thereby attaining liberation from the fever of afflictions.

Furthermore, if sentient beings commit various transgressions or offenses, one sets them aside and does not inquire into them; if one regards their respectful devotion and attachment with indifference rather than taking pleasure in them, this is the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*). These meanings of the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) are as explained in the Mahāyāna.
The Essential Explanation of the Dharma of Dhyāna, Volume One. Regarding pure contemplation (*śubha-vipaśyanā*), there are three grades:
those who have newly begun their practice, those who have already practiced it, and those who have practiced it for a long time.
If they are those who have newly begun their practice, one should instruct them as follows:

"Though the skin be broken, it is still impure; one should contemplate the person of white bones. Bind the mind to this contemplation so that it does not wander outward; if external thoughts arise regarding various conditions, restrain them and cause them to return."
If he has already practiced this, one should instruct him, saying:

"Withdraw the mind from the skin and flesh; observe the skull bone completely without allowing external thoughts to arise. If external thoughts regarding various conditions do occur, collect them and bring them back."
If one has practiced for a long time, one should withdraw [the mind] from the skin and flesh of the body by one inch and bind the attention to five locations:

the crown of the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the tip of the nose, and the heart region. By dwelling the attention on such places as these within the bones, one does not allow external thoughts to arise; should external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, one should collect them and bring them back.

One should further observe the mind: if the mind becomes exhausted, one should abandon all external perceptions and fix the attention upon the object of meditation. It is like a monkey tied to a pillar that runs about all day long, yet is constantly pulled back by its tether until it finally rests from exhaustion.
The object of focus is like a pillar, mindfulness is like a chain, and the mind is likened to a monkey.

It is also like a nurse who constantly watches over a small child to prevent them from falling; the practitioner’s observation of the mind is likewise. Gradually subduing the mind, one causes it to abide upon its object of focus. If the mind remains there for a long time, this accords with the method of dhyāna.

If one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), there are immediately three signs: the body becomes entirely harmonious, joyful, supple, and light; the white bones emit flowing light like white jade; and the mind attains a state of tranquil abiding—this is called the "pure contemplation" (*śubha-vipaśyanā*). At this time, one attains the mind of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*); this is known as the gateway to the method of practicing meditation for beginners.
If you have attained a superior state of concentration, it is better to restrain the mind and cause it to abide; this is called "one-pointedness of mind.
If you can cause it to abide for even a single inch [of time], you will then attain universal withdrawal; one must not merely contemplate a skeleton.

Having attained this contemplation, one sets aside the visualization of the red-boned person and contemplates the white-boned person, not allowing external thoughts to arise; if external thoughts concerning various conditions do occur, one gathers them back.

When the mind is pure and dwells in the contemplation of the bones, a white light from the sides of the bones issues forth throughout the body, like the extreme purity of sunlight on a clear, bright day.

Once this light has emerged, one observes it with the mind’s eye and perceives it clearly; by the power of that light, one sees the internal characteristics within the skeleton, resembling the arising and ceasing of various mental states and their associated factors, like water flowing through a tube of lapis lazuli. At that time, the mind becomes tranquil and attains bliss, such that the sensual pleasures of a lustful person cannot serve as a metaphor for it.
The contemplation of the external body is likewise so. Just as with the contemplation of a single body, one gradually increases the scope until it encompasses Jambudvīpa;
then, returning from that entire Jambudvīpa back to a single inch, the mind attains self-abiding. This is the samādhi-gate of purity within impurity.
Furthermore, this body is but a hollow skeleton covered by thin skin; what is there in it to find delight?
It is truly a source of great affliction.
*Chánfǎ yāojiě*, Scroll Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva and others of the Yao Qin dynasty at the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang’an:
If a practitioner wishes to seek the concentration of empty space, they should form this thought:
"Form is a manifold vessel of various sufferings; such as the suffering of being whipped, beaten, cut, killed, hunger, cold, old age, and illness—all these arise because of form.
By contemplating in this way, one abandons form and attains the sphere of infinite space.
Question: The practitioner currently takes form (rūpa) as their body; how can they then achieve its relinquishment? Answer:
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are the causes and conditions for form (*rūpa*), and they can also bind one to form; because these afflictions are extinguished, it is called "detachment from form.
Furthermore, by practicing the method of the contemplation of the voidness that destroys form, one attains detachment from form.

Furthermore, as the Buddha has taught, when a bhikṣu contemplates the five aggregates of the fourth dhyāna as being like a disease, an abscess, a wound, and a thorn—impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—such contemplations lead him to detach from the five aggregates of the fourth dhyāna. Because the remaining aggregates follow upon form (*rūpa*), it is said simply that he "detaches from form."
