Why is this? Because form is ultimately exhausted.

Furthermore, when the practitioner contemplates form, it is shattered part by part until no form remains; just as with the body, which has constituent parts—the head, feet, shoulders, arms, and so forth—each being a distinct part, there is no "body" apart from them.
If one were to separate the head into its constituent parts—such as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, mouth, beard, hair, bones, and flesh—the "head" would no longer exist.

Just as with the eye, which is a mass of flesh named "eye" resulting from the combination of ten factors—the four great elements, the four sense-objects, the body-faculty, and the eye-faculty—if these are each analyzed individually, the "eye" does not exist; the same applies to each of the constituent parts, such as earth and the other elements.
Question: Since the eye faculty is composed of the four great elements and its color cannot be definitively determined, how can it be distinguished? Answer:
The eye is defined as the conjunction of the four great elements and the translucent matter derived from them; if this matter were excluded, there would be no eye.
Furthermore, although this translucent matter is invisible, it possesses parts because it is resistant, and because it has parts, it is not the eye.
Furthermore, that which is able to see forms is called the eye;
if one excludes the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, there is no eye.
If it were the case that something could see forms without an eye, then the ear would also have to be the eye.
If the eye were a material phenomenon (rūpadharma), then because all material phenomena have location and parts, it would necessarily be divisible; if it were divisible, there would be many eyes.
If one says that the various subtle atoms (paramāṇu) produced by the four great elements constitute the eye, then there should not be a single eye;
yet if none of them were the eye, there would still not be a single eye.
If one says that the subtle atoms themselves are the eye, this is also not the case.
Why is this? If atoms possess form, they would have the ten directions and could not be called "atoms";
if they were formless, they could not be called "visible objects."
Furthermore, the substance of an atom is definitively composed of four parts:
color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility; yet the eye is not these four things. Why is this so?

The eye is comprised within the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), while the other four are comprised within the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*); for this reason, one cannot take atoms (*paramāṇu*) to be the eye.
As the Buddha taught, it is the conjunction of various factors that sees forms, which is conventionally designated as the "eye," yet it has no fixed reality;
the ear, nose, tongue, skin, flesh, bone, and so forth are likewise analyzed in this way.
This is the destruction of the internal characteristics of the body.
External forms, palaces, wealth, wives, children, and so forth are likewise all analyzed and destroyed in this manner.
As the Buddha told Rādha:
"From this day forward, one should disperse form and tear asunder form, so that no form remains.
To be able to discern in this way is called "detachment from form."

Furthermore, as the Buddha has taught: if a bhikṣu wishes to transcend form, pass beyond all signs of form, extinguish all signs of sensory opposition, and not attend to any signs of diversity, he enters the sphere of infinite space.
That which transcends all marks of form refers to visible form;
that which extinguishes all marks of resistance refers to obstructive yet invisible form;
and that which does not attend to any marks of difference refers to invisible and non-obstructive form.
Furthermore, "transcending all signs of form" refers to various signs of color such as blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple;
"extinguishing resistance" refers to sound, fragrance, taste, and touch;
and "not dwelling on any diverse signs" refers to large and small, long and short, square and round, far and near, and so forth.
Thus, having detached from all signs of form (*rūpa-nimitta*), one attains entry into the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Furthermore, the practitioner fixes the mind upon the internal spaces of the body—namely, the mouth, nose, throat, eyes, ears, chest, abdomen, and so forth. Having realized that form is a source of manifold afflictions while emptiness is free from distress, the mind takes delight in space. If the mind is dwelling on form, it is withdrawn and directed toward space; the mind becomes increasingly supple, causing the internal spaces within the body to gradually expand. One perceives one's own physical body as being like the holes in the root of a lotus. As this practice becomes sharper, one sees the entire body as empty, with no further form remaining.
External forms are also like this.

When internal and external space become one and the same space, the mind then takes that infinite and boundless space as its object; it thereby leaves behind perceptions of form and dwells in peace and happiness. It is like a bird in a jar that, upon the jar’s breaking, escapes and soars through the sky without any obstruction. This is called the first formless attainment (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

The practitioner regards form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being like a disease, an abscess, a sore, and a thorn; they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Seeking further for wondrous concentration, one then becomes detached from these objects of emptiness.

Why is this so? Because one knows that what is conceived by this mind—namely, empty space—is deceptive, illusory, and false; it was previously non-existent and now exists, and having existed, it returns to non-existence.
Having recognized its affliction, one realizes that this empty space arises from consciousness, yet one mistakenly regards consciousness as real.

One simply contemplates consciousness and relinquishes the object-condition of emptiness. When practicing the contemplation of consciousness, one gradually perceives that the characteristics of consciousness arise in succession, like a flowing stream or the flame of a lamp. The consciousness of the future, present, and past is a continuous succession of consciousness, boundless and immeasurable.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha say that the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) is boundless and immeasurable? Answer:
Consciousness is infinite because it can take distant objects as its conditions; it is infinite because it takes infinite phenomena as its conditions.

Furthermore, since it first takes infinite space as its condition, if that infinite space were destroyed, consciousness would likewise be infinite. Because the practitioner’s mind is supple, they are able to expand consciousness until it reaches infinity; this is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Question: Since this sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana) possesses all four aggregates (skandha), why is it called only the "sphere of consciousness"? Answer:
All internal phenomena have consciousness as their sovereign; all mental factors are subordinate to consciousness, such that when one speaks of consciousness, one is speaking of all other things.

Furthermore, within the desire realm, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is sovereign; within the form realm, the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha) is sovereign; in the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is sovereign; in the sphere of nothingness, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) is sovereign; and in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is sovereign.
Furthermore, there are three categories of phenomena:
the body, the mind, and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
In the desire realm and the form realm, the body is predominant because the mind follows the body; however, once the body is absent, the power of the mind functions independently.
The mind has two aspects:
one aspect takes emptiness as its object, and one aspect takes itself as its object; therefore, there should be two spheres:
the sphere of emptiness and the sphere of consciousness.
However, it is because form (*rūpa*) is first destroyed that space (*ākāśa*) receives its name; and because space is destroyed, consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone is given the name.
The mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) also have two parts:
one part is perception (*saṃjñā*) and one part is formations (*saṃskāra*); therefore, they too should have two locations.
One perceives the sphere of nothingness and practices in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, because one relies upon consciousness, one attains detachment from the sphere of infinite space; for this reason, although the other aggregates exist, it is consciousness alone that receives the name.

Once the practitioner has attained the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), they further seek a sublime concentration and contemplate consciousness as a source of affliction, as described above.

Furthermore, they contemplate that consciousness is like an illusion, deceptive, and dependent upon various causes and conditions, lacking autonomy; it arises when there are conditions and ceases when there are no conditions. Consciousness does not abide in the mind, nor does it abide in conditions, nor does it abide in between; it has no place of abiding, yet it is not without a place of abiding—such is the characteristic of consciousness.
The World-Honored One has said:
"Consciousness is like an illusion.
When the practitioner reflects in this way, they attain detachment from the sphere of consciousness.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects thus: "Just as the five desires are deceptive and false, so too is form;
just as form is deceptive and false, so too is space;
and just as space is deceptive and false, so too is the characteristic of consciousness."

All these are false and deceptive; yet sentient beings, being deluded and attached, take them to be all dharmas. Thinking that emptiness and non-existence are the place of peace and security, they form this thought and immediately enter the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Question: What is the difference between the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) and the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana)? Answer:
In the former case, one takes the perception of space as the object; in this case, one takes the perception of nothingness as the object—this is the distinction.

Once the practitioner has entered the sphere of nothingness, those of sharp faculties perceive that there are still feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within it, and thus become weary of them, as previously described;
those of dull faculties, however, are unable to perceive this.
Furthermore, there are three views that arise from the causal conditions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*):
the view of existence, the view of non-existence, and the view that is neither existence nor non-existence.
The view of existence extends from the desire realm up to the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*).
The view of non-existence is the sphere of nothingness;
the view of neither existence nor non-existence is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This view of non-existence should be abandoned.

Why is this? For even the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, though subtle, should still be abandoned; how much more so the sphere of nothingness? Having formed this thought, he detached himself from the sphere of nothingness.
Question: If within the Buddha-dharma there is also emptiness and non-existence, and if this is the reality, why do you say that wrong views should be abandoned? Answer:
Within the Buddha-dharma, things are taught as not being real for the purpose of destroying attachment;
yet, regarding the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one regards it as real due to the attachment of false views.

Once the sentient beings therein have experienced the fixed retribution, they again undergo various other retributions according to their karmic causes and conditions; for this reason, one should abandon [this state].
Although their names may be similar, their actual natures are each distinct.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects:

"All stages of perception (saṃjñā-bhūmi) are coarse and fraught with affliction; they are like a disease, an abscess, a wound, or an arrow. The stage of non-perception (asaṃjñā-bhūmi), however, is a state of delusion. Now, this is the tranquil, subtle, and supreme state, namely, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)."
Having observed in this way, one leaves behind the stage of the perception of nothingness and enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: Within this state, is there perception or is there no perception?
Answer: There is perception within this. Question:
If there is still perception (*saṃjñā*), why are only the lower seven stages designated as "stages of perception" (*saṃjñā-bhūmi*)?
The answer is:
because in these stages, perception is subtle and not sharp; since the functioning of perception is not fully clear, they are not called "perception."

The practitioner’s mind perceives this place as being neither with perception nor without perception; therefore, the Buddha, following its original name, calls it the "place of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

Those of dull faculties do not realize that within this there are four aggregates; they instead claim it to be the peaceful and secure place of nirvana, giving rise to overweening pride. After eighty thousand kalpas, their life ends and they fall back again into the various realms of existence.

Among these, although the four aggregates are subtle and profound, those of sharp faculties are able to perceive them. Having perceived them, they become weary and disenchanted, thinking: "These too are phenomena produced by a combination of factors;

phenomena born of causes and conditions are deceptive and unreal, like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, like an arrow. They are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Furthermore, they are the causes and conditions for future rebirth and should be abandoned. Because of this affliction, one should train in the Four Noble Truths."
Question: When abandoning the other stages, why is it not said that one trains in the Four Noble Truths? Answer:

Previously, by describing [the aggregates] as being like a disease, an abscess, a wound, and an arrow—impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—I have already briefly explained the Four Noble Truths, though I have not yet explained them in detail.
Furthermore, in other stages there are no obstructions or difficulties, as even ordinary beings on the path with outflows (*sāsrava*) can transcend them.
However, at this "summit of the world" (*bhavāgra*), only noble ones (*ārya*) practicing the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) are able to transcend it.
It is like a bird tied by its leg with a rope: although it may fly away at first, once the rope is exhausted, it is drawn back.
Ordinary persons are also like this; even if they pass through other stages, the King of Māras does not consider them a cause for alarm.
However, if they pass beyond the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the King of Māras is greatly alarmed, like a bird escaping when its rope snaps.
For this reason, the Four Truths are not taught when one is departing from other stages.
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the essential gateway to the three realms; those who wish to exit this gateway must study the Four Truths.
Question: What are the Four Noble Truths? Answer:
The truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
Suffering is of two kinds:
first, physical suffering; second, mental suffering.
Accumulation is also of two kinds:
first, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); second, the afflictions of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*).
Cessation is also of two kinds:
The first is nirvana with remainder, and the second is nirvana without remainder.
The Path is also of two kinds:
the first is concentration, and the second is wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of the Truth of Suffering:
first, suffering; second, the Noble Truth of Suffering.
As for suffering, it is characterized by affliction; that is to say, the five aggregates of clinging are called the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the noble truth of suffering: because one practices the path through knowledge and vision, it is called the noble truth of suffering.
There are two kinds of the truth of origination:
first, the truth of origination; second, the noble truth of origination.
The truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) has the characteristic of production; that is to say, the truths of afflictions such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth are called the truth of origination.
As for the noble truth of origination, it is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) by means of which [craving] is abandoned; this is the noble truth of origination.
The truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is of two kinds:
first, cessation (*nirodha*), and second, the noble truth of cessation (*ārya-nirodha-satya*).
Cessation refers to the characteristic of quiescent extinction, namely the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; this is called the truth of cessation.
Regarding the noble truth of cessation: because it is realized, one practices the path; this is the noble truth of cessation.
Regarding the truth of the path, there are two kinds:
first, the truth of the path, and second, the noble truth of the path.
The Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) has the characteristic of emerging and reaching [nirvāṇa], namely the Eightfold Noble Path; this is called the Truth of the Path.
As for the Noble Truth of the Path, it is the practice of the path through cultivation; this is the Noble Truth of the Path.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of truths:
general characteristics and specific characteristics.
Regarding the truth of suffering with respect to general characteristics, it consists of the five aggregates of clinging.

Regarding the suffering of specific characteristics (*pṛthag-lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*), it is the detailed analysis of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-skandha*).
Regarding the origin of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-samudaya*), it is that which can produce the sensations of future bodies.

Regarding the origin of specific characteristics (*pṛthag-lakṣaṇa-samudaya*), it is the detailed analysis of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and other afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as the causes and conditions of out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karman*) and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
As for cessation in its general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is the exhaustion of craving that gives rise to future existence;
as for cessation in its specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), it is the detailed differentiation of the ninety-eight types of exhaustion.
As for the path in its general characteristics, it is the Eightfold Noble Path.

Regarding the path of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-mārga*), it is extensively analyzed as extending from the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
If one does not penetrate the Four Noble Truths, one will revolve through the five destinies, wandering through birth and death without a moment’s rest.
For this reason, a practitioner should reflect that all afflictions, such as old age, sickness, and death, arise from the existence of a body, just as all grasses and trees grow from the earth.
As it is said in the sutras, the reason sentient beings throughout the ten directions possess bodies is that they are born solely for the purpose of undergoing suffering.
It is like poisoned food: whether excellent or vile, all serves to kill a person.
If one lacked both body and mind, there would be no locus for the suffering of death to reside.
Just as a violent wind breaks down a great tree, yet there is nothing to destroy if there is no tree;

so too, this is a brief explanation of the root of suffering for body and mind: just as space is the root of wind, wood is the root of fire, earth is the root of water, so the body is the root of suffering.

Furthermore, just as earth always has the characteristic of solidity, water always has the characteristic of moisture, fire always has the characteristic of heat, and wind always has the characteristic of motion, so too the body and mind always have the characteristic of suffering.
Why is this so? Because there is a body, the sufferings of old age, illness, death, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth constantly pursue it;
because there is a mind, the sufferings of sorrow, grief, fear, anger, vexation, jealousy, and so forth constantly pursue it.
If one knows that the body is suffering in the present, one knows that it was likewise so in the past; as it is with the body in the present and the past, so it will be in the future.
It is, for example, like seeing a grain seed now produce grain, whereby one infers that it was the same in the past and will be so in the future.
Furthermore, just as one uses the present characteristic of fire’s heat to infer that past and future fires are also hot,
so too, if there were no body or mind, there would have been no suffering in the past, there would be no suffering now, and there would be no suffering in the future.
One should know that the suffering of the three periods of time all arises from body and mind; therefore, one should contemplate the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Thus, when the mind gives rise to weary detachment, one sees that the causes and conditions of this suffering arise solely from afflictions such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and not from heaven, nor from time, nor spontaneously, nor without cause and condition. If one is free from afflictions, then birth does not occur.

One should know that the world arises entirely from afflictions such as craving; just as all human actions are preceded by desire, for this reason, the various afflictions are the causes and conditions of suffering.

Furthermore, it is by means of the water of craving that one receives a body; if there were no water of craving, one would not receive a body. It is like dry soil, which cannot adhere to a wall, but when mixed with water, it has something to which it adheres.

Furthermore, because of various afflictions (*kleśa*), one receives bodies that differ in many ways: those with much desire receive forms characterized by much desire; those with much hatred receive forms characterized by much hatred; those with much delusion receive forms characterized by much delusion; and those with thin afflictions receive forms with thin afflictions. Since one observes these differences in present retribution, one knows that past causes and conditions were each distinct. Likewise, in future lives, one receives different bodies according to one's afflictions, and similarly receives bodies according to one's karma.
If one does not give rise to hatred, one will not take the form of a venomous snake; the same applies to all other forms as well.

For this reason, one should know that craving and the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are the causes and conditions of all suffering. When the causes and conditions of suffering are exhausted, suffering is extinguished, which is *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is called "freedom from desire" (*vairāgya*); it is the severing of all afflictions, eternal and unchanging. Within it, there is no birth, no aging, no sickness, and no death; there is no suffering of being separated from what is loved, nor the suffering of encountering what is hated. It is constant bliss from which there is no falling back.
When the practitioner attains nirvana and liberation, there is nowhere to which they go; this is called "quiescent extinction" (śānta-nirvāṇa).
It is like lighting a lamp: when the oil is exhausted, it goes out and does not go to any direction. This is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).

Regarding the path of skillful means for attaining *nirvāṇa*, there are three divisions of concentration (*samādhi*), two divisions of wisdom (*prajñā*), and three divisions of ethical discipline (*śīla*); one dwells within this ethical discipline to practice concentration and wisdom.
That which is called wisdom capable of definitively discerning the Four Noble Truths is termed right view;
the awakening to and initiation of dharmas in accordance with right view constitutes right thought.
These are called the two factors of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right effort (*samyak-vīrya*) are called the three factors of concentration (*samādhi*).
Right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) are called the three factors of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Because one abides in pure ethical discipline, the sprouts of the various afflictions are prevented from growing; their power becomes diminished and thin, just as seeds sown out of season do not sprout. When the forces of the afflictions arise, they can certainly be obstructed by this factor, just as a great mountain damming water prevents the water from causing destruction.
For example, just as a mantra can neutralize a venomous snake so that its poison can no longer harm people, the fixed nature of things (*niyati*) is likewise.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) can uproot the very foundations of all afflictions (*kleśa*), just as during the summer floods when the waters surge, not a single tree on the riverbank remains unuprooted and swept away.

By practicing these three factors—the Eightfold Path—which is the true, direct, and correct road, one can extinguish the causes of suffering and attain ultimate peace, eternal bliss, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If one first practices its gateway through skillful means, there are ten matters:

first, the mind is single-mindedly correct; when various external circumstances arise to cause ruin, they cannot shift it, just as a mountain does not tremble even when winds blow from all four directions.

Second is integrity and straightforwardness: upon hearing the teacher’s exposition of the Dharma, one perceives neither its merits nor its flaws; the mind remains without increase or decrease, following the instruction without doubt. For example, when entering a dense forest to harvest timber, that which is straight emerges easily while that which is crooked is difficult to extract. Likewise, within the dense forest of the triple world, those who are straightforward emerge easily while those who are crooked find it difficult to emerge. Within the Buddha-dharma, only the straightforward is employed; the crooked is discarded.

Third is a sense of shame and dread of blame; this is the foremost and most excellent garment, the most sublime adornment. Shame and dread of blame act as hooks to restrain all evil thoughts. One who possesses both shame and dread of blame is truly a human being; one without shame and dread of blame is no different from a beast.

Fourth is heedfulness (*apramāda*), which is the root of all wholesome dharmas. Just as in the world one loses all beneficial matters through negligence, so too does a practitioner lose the benefit of *nirvāṇa* through negligence. One should know that negligence is like an enemy or a thief and always keep the mind far removed from it; one should know that heedfulness is like a sovereign, a father, or a teacher, and should follow and uphold it without abandoning it.

Fifth is seclusion: through this seclusion one achieves heedfulness; if one draws near to the five desires and the various sensory faculties become aroused, one should first physically distance oneself from villages and settlements, and subsequently mentally distance oneself by not dwelling on worldly affairs.
Sixth is having few desires: one does not seek many things for the necessities of life; for through seeking much, one falls into manifold afflictions. Seventh is contentment:

although a person may have few desires, if they take pleasure in and become attached to fine things, their aspiration for the Way will be ruined; therefore, the wise person seeks only what is sufficient.

Eighth, the mind should not be bound by attachment. Whether it be disciples, donors, acquaintances, or relatives—if they inquire after one's health, escort one, or involve one in many activities and affairs—such things destroy the Path; therefore, one should not be bound by attachment.

Ninth, they take no pleasure in worldly delights—such as singing, dancing, and music, or selecting auspicious times and favorable days for good fortune—but find no joy in any such mundane affairs whatsoever.
Tenth is patience. When a practitioner seeks the Way, they should practice patience regarding ten matters:

first, harassment by mosquitoes and gadflies; second, stings from snakes and vipers; third, venomous beasts; fourth, verbal abuse and slander; fifth, physical assault and injury; sixth, illness and pain; seventh, hunger; eighth, thirst; ninth, cold; and tenth, heat. Regarding such afflictions, the practitioner must endure them and not allow themselves to be overcome; they must always prevail over these circumstances.

Furthermore, it is like a person who recognizes the symptoms of an illness, understands the causes and conditions of the illness, knows the medicine that removes the illness, and obtains a caregiver; thus, whatever they require will be provided as desired, and they shall recover before long.

The practitioner who thus knows the true characteristic of suffering, knows the causes and conditions of suffering, knows the path to the cessation of suffering, and knows how to obtain a virtuous teacher and fellow students, will before long attain peace and nirvana.

Question: Having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entered deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one’s fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the higher realms are already attenuated and the mind is supple; should one not then contemplate these Four Noble Truths through various causes, conditions, and parables? Such [a requirement] seems as if it implies a lack of faith.

The answer is: It is not only for those at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) that this is taught; it is taught generally for all beings at the Peak of Existence. One simply contemplates the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—like a disease, like an ulcer, like an arrow piercing the heart. These [aggregates], being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) produced by causes and conditions and are thus deceptive. One contemplates *nirvāṇa* as supremely sublime, peaceful, and blissful—not a conditioned phenomenon, but real and non-deceptive. By extinguishing the three poisons and the three decays, the suffering of body and mind is extinguished. Constantly censuring the four aggregates and their causes and conditions is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Praising *nirvāṇa* and the path to *nirvāṇa* is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

When a practitioner attains the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, the mind becomes supple; if they seek the five supernormal powers, they will attain them easily by relying on the fourth dhyāna. Although they may also attain them by relying on the first, second, or third dhyānas, it is extremely difficult to seek them there, and even if attained, they will not be stable.

Why is this? Because in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra disturb the concentration; in the second dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is excessive; and in the third dhyāna, bliss (*sukha*) is excessive—all of which are contrary to concentration. The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are all characteristics of concentration. Only in the fourth dhyāna is there neither suffering nor pleasure, neither sorrow nor joy, and no inhalation or exhalation; it is the abode of the noble ones, characterized by happiness and tranquility. Therefore, the practitioner should rely upon the fourth dhyāna to cultivate the four bases of psychic power.

That is to say, when one achieves mastery over the practice of the concentration of desire, and achieves mastery over the practices of the concentration of diligence, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation, there is nothing that cannot be attained by one who dwells in reliance upon these.
Question: How does one accomplish the practice of the dharma of concentration through desire so that it accords with one's wishes? Answer:

"Desire" (chanda) refers to the longing for the object sought; "concentration" (samādhi) refers to one-pointedness of mind without increase or decrease. The term "practice of the dharma" (dharmacaryā) refers to faith, resolve, skillful wisdom, joy, and gladness, which assist in accomplishing desire and concentration. Because desire acts as the primary cause by which concentration is attained, it is called "desire-concentration" (chandha-samādhi).
The same applies to "effort-concentration," "mind-concentration," and "investigation-concentration."

The practitioner contemplates desire so that it neither increases nor decreases; he ensures that it is not overly withdrawn within nor overly scattered without, but is supple, balanced, harmonized, and functional—just like tuning a lute for its strings' tension and slackness, so that whatever melody is played may be performed.
Vigor (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) are likewise. For example, when a practitioner trains in flying, the desire to fly is called "desire" (*chanda*).
Gathering the distracted mind and collecting the factors that assist the practice is called "vigor-mind" (*vīrya-citta*).

Being able to lift the body and depart from the physical and mental heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), such as sleep and agitation, so that the mind becomes light and agile—because the mind is light, it can lift the body—is called "mind" (*citta*).

To deliberate upon the degree of one’s desire and diligence, being able to sustain the body yet not yet having destroyed the internal and external flavors of form—this is called contemplation (*cintā*).
By relying on the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), one can fulfill all merits; how much more so the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*)!
Question: Among the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), which arises first? Answer:
That which is preferred comes first. Question:
If that is so, why is the supernormal power of transformation placed at the beginning?
Answer: The five supernormal powers are mostly for the sake of sentient beings. Why is this so?
Just as an Arhat liberated by wisdom, having attained Arhatship, reflects thus:

"There are sentient beings with dull faculties who do not believe in the Way and treat the Buddha-dharma with contempt. I have achieved this difficult feat of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows; why should I not employ these supernormal powers to transform sentient beings and prevent them from falling into sin?"
Furthermore, the Buddha’s great compassion benefits all sentient beings; as his disciple, I ought to assist and benefit them through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Now, most sentient beings derive benefit from manifest phenomena, and when spiritual transformations move the masses—both noble and humble—all without exception bow down in submission. Among the other supernormal powers, none possess such efficacy.
For this reason, the supernormal power of transformation is placed first.
It is asked:
Since the bodies of devas abound in fire and heat, they possess natural radiance and are also able to ascend into the void and travel swiftly; why is this not mentioned here?
Because ghosts and spirits consist mostly of wind, their bodies are light and swift, encountering no obstruction;
because dragons consist mostly of water, mental thoughts produce water and they can also undergo transformations;
because human beings consist mostly of earth, they have little of the characteristic of light movement—how, then, can they fly?
The answer is:

Because the earth-element of the human body possesses little of the characteristic of lightness and mobility, one seeks to learn supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). If one were like a celestial being or a spirit, what would be the use of such powers?
Just as the earth, though heavy, moves due to the power of water, so too, by the power of the mind, one is able to lift one's own body.

For example, when a monkey falls from a great height it does not injure its body, whereas a human falling from the same height would be wounded; this is because the monkey’s mental power is so light, swift, and robust that it remains unhurt.
One should know that the supernormal power of the body is likewise so, because the power of the mind is strong.
Furthermore, it is like a person who can swim; although they are in deep water, they do not sink because the power of their mental skillful means enables them to support their own body.
For this reason, one should know that although the human body is heavy, because the power of the mind is strong, the body flies through the void.
Question: If this is thus to be believed, how should one train? Answer:

If a practitioner dwells in the fourth dhyāna, relying on the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they concentrate their mind with single-minded mindfulness to contemplate that every part of the body is empty like the holes within a lotus root. Taking up the signs of lightness and agility, they practice them without ceasing until body and mind merge, like iron merging with fire. Thus, the coarse characteristics of the body are extinguished, leaving only a body of lightness and agility.

Through union with desire, diligence, intention, and the auxiliary factors of practice, by the power of these wholesome practices such as desire, the body follows [the mind] just as fire functions within the light and pliant iron.

Furthermore, the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta) of the form realm (rūpadhātu) is conjoined with this body, causing the body to become light and agile so that it can move according to one's will.
It is like when a person takes medicine: it causes the mind to become clear and the body to become light and agile.
For example, the derived matter produced by the four great elements in the realm of form is luminous and pure;

because it resides within this body, the eyes are likewise luminous and pure. It is like a person learning to jump: through practice, they become increasingly skilled until they surpass all others. Or like a fledgling bird learning to fly, which gradually increases its distance;
the supernormal power of the body is thus: when first attained, it may cover one or two *zhang*, but gradually one becomes able to fly further.
These supernormal powers of transformation are of four kinds:

first, flying through the air like a bird; second, making the distant near; third, vanishing from here and appearing there; fourth, moving as swiftly as thought—within the span of a single thought-moment, which consists of sixty instants, one can traverse immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, arriving immediately upon the arising of that thought.

By means of these supernormal powers, the body attains mastery: one body can become many bodies, and many bodies can become one body; the large can become small, and the small can become large; it can be as heavy as Mount Sumeru or as light as a goose feather—such are the deeds performed according to one's will.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power of the body, they traverse as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in a single thought-moment. Yet, while sentient beings see the bodhisattva arrive at those places, the bodhisattva does not move from their original location; furthermore, their preaching of the Dharma and teaching of beings there is never interrupted.

There may be gods and humans who are attached to the inversion of permanence; for those who can be delivered through supernatural powers, he manifests the burning of the trichiliocosm, such that sentient beings see the trichiliocosm being consumed by fire and destroyed, yet the land itself suffers no damage.

There are sentient beings who give rise to arrogance; [the Bodhisattva] manifests as one holding a vajra in his hand, from which fire issues forth from the vajra. Those who see this are struck with fear and submit, paying homage with reverence.

If there are those who delight in and are attached to the body of a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*), he immediately manifests as a wheel-turning sage king to preach the Dharma for them; or he may manifest as Śakra Devānām Indra, or as a Māra king, or as a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or as the body of a Buddha—preaching the Dharma according to whichever body they find pleasing.
Alternatively, the Bodhisattva may sit cross-legged in mid-air, emitting various kinds of light from all four sides of his body while preaching the Dharma.

Or, when sentient beings delight in diverse and colorful adornments, he immediately manifests for them a trichiliocosm adorned with the seven treasures—complete with banners, streamers, flower canopies, and a hundred varieties of musical instruments—and preaches the Dharma from within it.
Alternatively, he may cause the trichiliocosm to become a single ocean of water, covered with blue and red lotuses, and preach the Dharma upon them;
or he may sit atop Mount Sumeru and preach the Dharma with the Brahma-voice, which is heard throughout all lands.
At times, sentient beings do not see his form, but hear only the sound of him preaching the Dharma.
Or he manifests in the body of a gandharva, using the sounds of music and song to gladden their hearts, and only thereafter preaches the Dharma.
Or they manifest as dragon kings with thunder and lightning to preach the Dharma.
Through such various causes, conditions, and skillful means, they display spiritual transformations to attract and guide sentient beings.
Question: These supernatural transformations of various objects—how is it that they are not false? Answer:

The practitioner first realizes that all phenomena are false and deceptive, like illusions and transformations. For example, it is like molding clay to create whatever one desires; even those with merit can cause snow to fall in summer, flowers to bloom in winter, or rivers to cease flowing. Furthermore, when a rishi is provoked to anger, he can transform tigers, wolves, and lions into stone bodies—how much more so can one who possesses supernatural powers and meditative concentration not transform objects?

Furthermore, within all things there are respective elemental components (*dhātu*). By taking up these component characteristics and expanding them through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), the others vanish.

As it is said in the Sūtra: there was a bhikṣu who had attained mastery over his mind through supernormal power; seeing a large piece of wood, he wished for it to become earth, and it immediately became entirely earth.
Why is this so? Because wood has the element of earth as its constituent part.
It is the same for water, fire, and wind.
If one fashions various precious objects such as gold and silver, one may do so according to one's will. Why is this?
Because wood possesses a pure portion.
Question: Since the transformation of things is thus, and their manifestation has neither beginning nor end, what is the nature of this matter? Answer:

Some say that within empty space there are subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) composed of the four great elements; through the power of transformation, these atoms are caused to combine and form a transformed person (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*).

This is like how, when a person dies, they may be reborn in the heavens or in hell due to the causes and conditions of their transgressions or merits; the combination of atoms to form a transformation is likewise such a phenomenon of the supernatural power of material transformation.

If a practitioner seeks to attain the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), they likewise take the fourth dhyāna as the foundation and cultivate the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) as previously described. Having made their mind supple and pliant, they focus their mindfulness upon the sounds of the great assembly and apprehend the various characteristics of sound. Whatever sounds are heard, they should constantly maintain mental attention toward them; if the mind wanders to other objects, they should restrain it and bring it back. By constantly practicing single-minded mindfulness, they will, within the ear itself, obtain a pure form produced by the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). This is called the cultivation of the divine ear.

By means of this divine ear, one hears the sounds in immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions—namely, the voices of devas, humans, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, caṇḍālas, and mahoragas—as well as the voices of animals, hungry ghosts, and the coarse, subtle, great, and small sounds of the suffering in the hells; all these are heard.

As the Bodhisattva’s concentrated mind becomes increasingly profound, he hears the voices of the Buddhas of the ten directions; hearing the Dharma from the Buddhas, he does not grasp at signs. He regards the Dharma as the true Dharma and the supreme, relying on its profound meaning rather than on the words.
What is the profound meaning?
It is said to be knowing that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless, and thus not giving rise to false views.

Within this meaning, one does not even apprehend "meaning," and within that which is unapprehendable, there is no characteristic of apprehension. This is relying on the profound meaning and not relying on words.
Furthermore, the practitioner relies on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and does not rely on sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
As for sūtras of definitive meaning: if one can rely upon the meaning, then all sūtras are of definitive meaning, because that meaning is ultimately empty and possesses an ineffable character.
Therefore, all sutras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
If one does not rely on their meaning, that person regards all sutras as being of non-definitive meaning. Why is this so?

Because they lack profound wisdom and merely follow after sounds, [they do not realize that] the true nature of these sounds also enters into the profound meaning; both are inexpressible. This is called the discrimination of sūtras of definitive meaning and those that are not of definitive meaning.
Furthermore, the practitioner relies on wisdom (*jñāna*) and does not rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*). Why is this?

The practitioner knows that this characteristic of consciousness arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions; it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), is formless, non-obstructive, and invisible; it is devoid of cognition and awareness, and is deceptive like an illusion.
Thus, regarding the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*), when consciousness itself becomes wisdom (*jñāna*), one relies upon wisdom and not upon consciousness.

Although a practitioner may give rise to consciousness—whether it be consciousness or wisdom—they do not produce attachment to it. They understand that the characteristics of consciousness are themselves the characteristics of wisdom; they then teach this characteristic of wisdom to sentient beings.
Furthermore, the practitioner relies on the Dharma and not on the person.

Why is this? If there were truly a "person" within the Buddha's teachings, there would be no one who attains purity or liberation; yet all phenomena are without self and without person. It is only for the sake of conforming to worldly convention that one speaks of a person or a self. For this reason, the practitioner relies on the Dharma and not on the person.

That which is called "Dharma" is the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). The nature of phenomena is the nature of non-arising; this nature of non-arising is ultimate emptiness; and this ultimate emptiness is that which is ineffable.

Why is this? Because the Dharma is taught through speech, yet within the Dharma there is no speech, and within speech there is no Dharma. Speech is itself the characteristic of non-speech; all verbal expressions lack the characteristic of being verbal expressions. For this reason, the Sūtra says: "That which is neither demonstrated nor preached is called the Buddha-Dharma."

The practitioner hears the teachings of all Buddhas with the divine ear; yet regarding either persons or dharmas, they do not give rise to views of attachment. If one discriminates between two characteristics, that is not the Buddha-dharma; if there are no two characteristics, that is the Buddha-dharma.

By relying on the power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), the practitioner hears the most profound Dharma and thereby teaches and transforms sentient beings; this is called the supernormal power of the divine ear.

If the practitioner wishes to attain the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), they first observe their own mind, grasping its characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. They also understand the characteristics of the mind’s defilement and purity, as well as its states of concentration and distraction. Furthermore, they observe the objects of the mind’s perception, including their defilement or purity, proximity or distance, and quantity.

Having already grasped the internal and external mental characteristics, he observes the forms of sentient beings and grasps the mind characterized by desire, the mind characterized by hatred, the mind characterized by pride, the mind characterized by stinginess, the mind characterized by envy, the mind characterized by sorrow, the mind characterized by fear, and the minds characterized by various activities such as speech and sound. He then reflects:
"As with my own mind, so it is with that [the Buddha]—at the time of arising, at the time of abiding, and at the time of ceasing, he is likewise."
"One knows for oneself the objects of one's own mind, and others are likewise so.
My mind possesses such signs of form, speech, and activity, and others are likewise so."

One constantly cultivates and studies the characteristics of the mind; having practiced in this way, one attains the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others. At that time, one takes only the minds and mental factors of others as objects, just as one with clear vision observes fish in pure water, seeing them all—whether large or small, beautiful or ugly—even though they are covered by water, for the water being pure does not constitute an obstruction.

The practitioner is likewise; by virtue of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, they are able to perceive the minds of sentient beings even when those minds are concealed by their bodies. Having attained this supernormal power of mind, they may at times preach the Dharma in a great assembly; first understanding the minds of others, they know with what profound intention these sentient beings act, what dharmas they practice, what causes and conditions they possess, what marks they bear, and what matters they delight in. Because they know their own mind to be pure, they know that the minds of sentient beings can likewise be purified.

Just as in a clean mirror, whatever forms appear—whether long or short, square or round, coarse or fine—they manifest according to their original characteristics, neither increasing nor decreasing. Why is this so?
Because a mirror is pure and clear, although the mirror does not engage in discrimination, it manifests their forms.
It is the same for the practitioner: because one's own mind is pure, all phenomena lack any fixed characteristic, for they are eternally pure.

He fully knows all the primary minds and mental factors of sentient beings; if there are many in the assembly who possess lustful desires, he immediately knows their minds and preaches for them the Dharma for transcending lustful desire. It is the same for anger and delusion.
Why is this? Because the true nature of the mind is without attachment, without hatred, and without delusion.
If there are those among the assembly who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas, he likewise knows their minds and teaches the Dharma for them.
Although he preaches the Dharma for them, he knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is likewise without smallness.
For those who seek the path of a pratyekabuddha, he also knows their minds and preaches the Dharma for them;
although he preaches the Dharma for them, he knows that the nature of phenomena is likewise without a middle.
If there are those who seek the Mahāyāna, he also knows their minds and preaches the Dharma for them;
though he preaches the Dharma, he knows that the nature of dharmas has no greatness.
The practitioner, in this way, preaches the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings with equanimity, yet does not discriminate among the characteristics of the mind.
Although they teach the Dharma by distinguishing the three vehicles, they do not disrupt the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
because they do not disrupt the nature of phenomena, they fully know the mental activities of all sentient beings.

Although they use their own minds to know the minds of others, they experience neither opposition nor compliance toward those minds; furthermore, they know that the succession of the minds of all sentient beings is like the flow of a stream.

Just as one knows the nature of the mind, so too is the nature of phenomena; by knowing the minds of sentient beings with the knowledge of others' minds, one preaches the Dharma for them, and thus does no harm—this is called the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds.

If a practitioner wishes to know their past lives, they should first become aware of the events of the present, then the events of the recent past, proceeding back through last night, yesterday, and the day before; in this manner, they should trace back one month, from the current year back to childhood—just as one who travels a road, upon reaching their destination, reflects upon and recollects all the places they have passed through on the journey.

Having practiced in this way, because they have skillfully cultivated the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they remember the time of birth and the time of dwelling in the womb; they know of dying in such-and-such a place and being born into this womb, and they know one lifetime, two lifetimes, three lifetimes, and even up to a hundred lifetimes, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, immeasurable, and billions of lifetimes.

By means of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), they personally know their own bodies and those of others throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, recollecting and knowing them all.
They teach and transform sentient beings through these matters of past lives, speaking thus:
"In such-and-such a place, I had such-and-such a name and clan, such-and-such a birth, such-and-such a lifespan, and experienced such-and-such suffering and joy."
He also recounts the events that occurred to them.

By means of the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), the practitioner knows the causes and conditions of the sins and merits of these sentient beings in previous existences—namely, the causes and conditions for becoming a śrāvaka, the causes and conditions for becoming a pratyekabuddha, and the causes and conditions for becoming a buddha—and he teaches the Dharma to them in accordance with those causes and conditions.

Furthermore, by virtue of the power of knowing past lives, the practitioner realizes that although they have planted roots of goodness under various Buddhas, they did not dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; now, they shall dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The practitioner also knows that when past phenomena cease, they go nowhere; and they know that when future phenomena arise, they come from nowhere.
Although they know that the past has no beginning, they do not give rise to the view of a beginningless [self];
although they contemplate that sentient beings of the future will pass away and enter nirvana, they likewise do not give rise to the view of extremes.
When the practitioner recollects past lives, he increases all roots of goodness and extinguishes the causes and conditions of offenses from immeasurable lifetimes.
Why is this? Because he knows that all phenomena have neither new characteristics nor old characteristics.

Having attained such wisdom, one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the suffering and pleasure experienced throughout the cycle of birth and death as being like what is seen in a dream. For this reason, one does not give rise to weariness toward birth and death, but instead arouses a heart of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*) for all sentient beings. Knowing that all phenomena possess the characteristic of being constructed (*kṛtaka-lakṣaṇa*), one reflects:

"Just as my coming and going through birth and death over countless billions of immeasurable eons has been entirely false and unreal, so too is the coming and going of all sentient beings through birth and death."
"If the four great elements and the four aggregates did not exist, that would be reality; yet even these four great elements and four aggregates are ultimately unarisen.

Furthermore, the practitioner, through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), recollects that the pleasures once experienced as a Cakravartin King were impermanent and subject to destruction; the pleasures of Śakra Devendra were likewise impermanent and subject to destruction. Even the pure and magnificent adornments of various lands, the sublime forms of bodhisattvas and Buddhas, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma—all are entirely impermanent; how much more so other matters?
Having reflected thus, the mind becomes weary and detached.

Relying on the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), the practitioner enters into impermanence and emptiness; they contemplate how all phenomena are empty and impermanent, yet sentient beings, due to their inversions, remain attached to them.
For the sake of these sentient beings, one gives rise to a mind of compassion; by practicing this compassion, one gradually attains great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Having attained great compassion, the Buddhas of the ten directions keep this bodhisattva in mind and praise their virtue; this is called the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*).

If a practitioner wishes to attain the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they should first take up the signs of luminous light, namely lamps, fire, bright pearls, the sun, the moon, the stars, and so forth.
Having taken up these signs of light, if it is daytime, they should close their eyes; at night, they should maintain the mental image of that luminous sign as if seen by the eye.
One constantly cultivates clear mindfulness, binding the mind to clarity so that no other thoughts arise; if they do wander away, one gathers them back to bring the mind to a single point.

At this time, the pure form produced by the four great elements of the form realm (rūpadhātu) exists within these eyes; this is called the "divine eye" (divyacakṣus). It is called the divine eye because it is produced by the four great elements of the gods, and it is also called the divine eye because it is the pure eye of the noble ones (ārya).

Once the practitioner has attained this divine eye, mountains, trees, the Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Sumeru, and all lands present no obstruction whatsoever; with this unimpeded eye, they are able to see the infinite, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions and their adorned lands.
At that time, the practitioner is able to know that all Buddhas are one Buddha, and also sees that one Buddha is all Buddhas, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indestructible.
Just as he perceives the marks of the Buddhas, he likewise perceives the marks of his own body.
Because the characteristics of one's own body are pure, the characteristics of all phenomena are likewise so.
Just as the Buddha is seen to be pure, the disciple is also thus; there are no two distinct characteristics.

Furthermore, regarding the sentient beings in the immeasurable lands of the ten directions—whether in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or devas—with the exception of those in the formless realm—he sees all their births and deaths, both beautiful and ugly. He fully knows the karmic causes, conditions, and retributions of the sentient beings within the six destinies of the ten directions:

that these sentient beings are born among devas and humans due to the causes and conditions of wholesome karma, while those sentient beings are born in the three evil paths due to the causes and conditions of unwholesome karma.

Because the practitioner has attained the power of wisdom within the divine eye, although they see sentient beings, they do not give rise to the notion of "sentient beings," for all dharmas are devoid of the notion of sentient beings;
although they see the continuity of karma and its retribution, they also enter into the state where all dharmas are without karma and without retribution.
Although he sees all forms with the divine eye, by the power of wisdom he does not grasp at the marks of form, for all such forms are entirely empty.
Furthermore, whether obstructed or unobstructed, near or far, above or below, there is nothing he does not see.

When the practitioner sees the pure and subtle forms of the various devas of the form realm, they do not see them; even the Great Devas (Mahādeva) likewise cannot be seen.
